entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: September 18, 1990 Interview

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following transcript was made from a recorded interview with Jake Rohner that took place at Jake 's home on September 18, 1990. Due to some problems with the recording equipment, about 40 minutes of the interview--between Part I and Part Hfailed to record. After reviewing the transcripts, Joke and Willie provided written corrections and additions. These comments appear throughout the manuscript enclosed in [brackets] and include the initials of the person that has provided the information.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. Coffin Butte Neighborhood

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The first thing I'd like you to describe Jake, is when your father came over from Switzerland, and how your father and mother came to live in Oregon.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, my father's mother's brother migrated, came to Kansas. Settled in Kansas. And then if any of the family that wanted to come over, he would send the money for them to come over. And there were ten in father's family, and five came one by one to Kansas and settled there. And this was in 1908, when my father caine. In 1913 he went back to Switzerland and brought my mother over to Kansas, and my mother said, "This is not for me!" Dry, and windy, and no trees. So he said, let's go to Oregon then. So they came to Oregon, and ended up in Washougal, Washington working for Mr. Writsman, and after a while there he said, "Would you like to rent my farm there near Coffin Butte?" So they looked at it, they made a deal, they rented the farm. Which is known as the Writsman Place. And so all of our family, the older family members were born on that place, and I'm the oldest of the family. Just at the base of Coffin Butte, and the road to our farm came off of Highway 99 and it was our own private road back to the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On your uncle [Great Uncle Kobler], do you know what year he came to Kansas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't, but it must have been quite a few years earlier because all his family, his children, were born in Kansas. And they were about the same, roughly the same age as my father.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know why your father caine to Kansas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he wanted a piece of the new world, I guess you could call it. And so he came and worked for about five years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the name of your father's mother? Do you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Last name?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Kobler.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so the uncle in Kansas was Kobler?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Fact is we had the family reunion.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kobler family reunion?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there is quite afew Koblers in the northwest?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, in the northwest now, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall your mother's parents names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hasler.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hasler. And so did your mother and father know each other in Switzerland?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I'm sure they did, before my father went back. Because they were from two towns about four miles apart. Small, very small towns.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you tell me the name of those towns?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Allstatten. My mother was from Allstatten, and my father from Montlingen, which was just.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how they came to the United States?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: By boat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know the name of the boat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. And they got terribly seasick. And dad laughed about it many times. He said, "We quit on fish, and we started in on fish again," which was on Friday. See, they got sick on Friday, and then the next Friday they started eating again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were Catholic.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And very seasick.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how they came from New York to Kansas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I suppose by train; I'm sure on train.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you think the same from Kansas to Oregon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how he met Writsman?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not positive, but I think through the employment agency. He had a dairy and this was an employment agency, so they applied for the job and got the job.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know Writsman 's first name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could it have been Francis?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Could have been anything - I just don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, then when your father came down and rented the Writsman 's Place, that's what it was known as?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were telling me you were born in the house that's showing in the [Soap Creek Auto Tour. OSU Research Forests. 1989. p.1O.]tour book?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall anything about that house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well it was a big house. Two story. And the family picture is of the house. [This refers to the picture shown on the title page.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall what happened to that house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It burned down years later. A Russian man, by the name of Mike Dobrinin, and there were quite a few Dobrinins in the Peoria/Halsey area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you recall about the Barzees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, just neighbors, and we used to work back and forth somewhat, like on thrashing duties. Roy Barzee that lived close to Glenders, he had two girls and a boy. And then there was Lester, he lived across from Adair Village which was a little bit north. And his wife was a school teacher, and she was one of my school teachers. In grade school. [School teachers were hired a year at a time, and at the end of the year the teacher would go around to each School Board member and see whether she should be re-hired or not. JR]
bracketed_corrections: [School teachers were hired a year at a time, and at the end of the year the teacher would go around to each School Board member and see whether she should be re-hired or not. JR]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was her name Barzee?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Edith Barzee.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And she taught school at...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At Wells. For I think maybe two years while I was there. In those days they didn't

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: hire teachers but only for one year at a time. You see every spring the teachers would come and apply for jobs. And then the Board would pick somebody. So we nearly always had a new teacher every year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the Hoffinans?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What can you recall about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, not much. They were both rather short people and he was kind of a comical fellow. I liked to visit with him. Of course I was quite young back them, that was before we ever left Camp Adair. And he had a small farm, a little timberland on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you say he was short, on Hoffman, how short is that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know. As I remember it seemed to me like neither one was much over 5 feet. Probably were a little, but seemed short.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they local people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know how long they had lived there. They were there ever since I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then he did a little farming and owned a little timber.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall the Blakes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, yes. She was also one of my teachers one year in school. And I think she did a little substitute teaching in between when the teacher was sick or something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you recall about Mr. Blake?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, he was a nice old gentleman. That's about all I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. How about Joe Smith?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Joe Smith, yes, yes. Fact is, my father bought 112 acres which had a barn and house on it; he bought it from Joe Smith there by Coffm Butte.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there other farmers in that area where you moved to, other than Joe Smith at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, there were farmers all around us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall their names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well there was the Stambaughs to the west of us, and Mackeys and later the Armstrongs, and north of us on Walter Wiles place was Wesley Kester. And on our

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: lane, we shared our lane with Mr. and Mrs. Eston Carter. [Eston Carter's house burned down during the dust storm in the spring of 1930 or '31. It was red dust and a stiff wind from the northeast. We were planting potatos southwest of Carter's and charred shingles blew 1/4 to 1/2 mile toward us. It got quite dark with the red dust and Mom got scared, it was so eerie. Eston Carter's son, Lyle, used to live in Sisters, but may live in the Redmond area now. He moved there in 1942. JR} At the foot of the butte toward the highway. And the Steilmachers joined our place on the east. And then the Schulmericks also on the east.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall the Sheppards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. John Sheppard?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. What can you recall about him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I remember the older gentleman, John Sheppard, and then the son, John, who was older than I. And I think there was maybe a sister I believe, well oh yes, I think that was Mrs. Griffin that lived on Marcks place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Mrs. Griffin lived on Marc/cs place? So they moved there after Mrs. Marc/cs moved out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know whether they moved there directly after or after somebody else, but they were there a few years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they purchase the place from Mrs. Marc/cs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know whether they purchased it or rented it. I couldn't say.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the Folks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, Bert Folks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you recall about him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, not a whole lot either. We didn't associate but I knew him and he lived next to his property joined Joe Smith's property.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're kind of getting closer to your family there, just kind of the outer limits of those people. But do you recall any of the people out towards Airlie or Berry Creek? Any of the families in those areas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I heard my mother talk about the Shanks and the Kilmers, which lived from the Writsman place just northwest.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the Kilmers, they lived across the road from the Writsman 'S Place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just up the road toward Airlie a little bit. How far I don't know, but right in

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could they have lived on the other side of Smith Hill or Folks Hill, or were they on the Soap Creek side, the Kilmers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't think they were very far from the Writsman place, so it would be near Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's. . . at the base of Writsman 's Hill, the hill we were describing, it would be west of the Writsman 's place, there is a creek and an old orchard and some old buildings there. Or there were in the 1930's. On the other side of the road; on the west side of the road. Can you recall a family that lived in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't know where the Kilmers or the Shanks lived, but it's somewhere through that area. And of cQurse Jim Hanish and his family lived out in there somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know the Hanishes at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not until 30 years ago. Maybe closer to 40.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Problem with the tape recorder resulted in 40-minute gap.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 2. Studack Accident

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, you were describing hearing about Studack's accident in the woods.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, father and mother and my sisters and I, we were digging potatoes, I think probably the middle of October or toward the later part, in the southwest corner of our farm, joining Beals farm and the Wiles farm, when somebody came to notify, tell us, about the Mr. Studack being injured in the woods. And he wasn't expected to live.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did. . .how old were you then? That was 1928, so you would have been.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: 1928, I would have been 14. I was born in 1914.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you remember seeing him in the hospital?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I remember the family going to visit him in the hospital, but he was unconscious and he wasn't expected to live. And it was in Dr. Anderson's hospital, when Dr. Anderson had his own hospital in Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: At that time then, he had a pregnant wife and three children and his best friend living on the property?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he was boarding with them I believe at the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Zundt?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Albert Zundt, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Mr. Zundt ever get married?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he was a bachelor.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 3. Local Folks and Legends

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Folks lived at the base of a hill. Did you have a name for that hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What my folks?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, the Folks family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, the Folks family. No, I don't remember a name for that hill. But it was just before you got to the Joe Smith property. Right across from the Joe Smith property.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, next to Joe Smith there is a large swamp and kind of a lake. Do you remember a name for that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. All I know is Berry Creek run through Joe Smith's place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear the name Savage Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or Forest Peak? Or Bakers Mountain or the Baker family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we've talked about Coffin Butte. Can you remember a hill behind the Glenders?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I remember a hill behind the Glenders, but I don't know whether it had a name or not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. There is Soap Creek, can you remember any of the names for any of the small creeks that entered into Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I can't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, when you started school. Your first year, that was at Wells?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At Welisdale, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said you couldn't speak English at that time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any other kids that couldn't speak English?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I was the only one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that create any problems?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it didn't. I pIcked it up real fast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any problems with the other kids because of a German accent at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were a little younger than I, so they picked it up pretty fast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was no political problems because of World War I, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any black people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, only one, and that was in later years in Corvallis. I can't even think of his name right now, but he was well known around Corvallis. Bud, I think was his name, Bud Smith.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bud Smith? But that's the only black you could remember. What do you remember about him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, he was just a plain nice fellow. He wasn't, probably very little older than I.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would he do for a living?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he shined shoes and things like that. Earlier. I don't know what he did later. Fact is, I think he worked some for Penneys if I remember right, J.C. Penneys, when my wife worked there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any Indian people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I never knew any Indians.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Orientals?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just once in Corvallis, at a chinese restaurant. That's all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the racial mix was almost entirely white people.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Entirely white people, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there ever be black visitors or Indian visitors to town that you can recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there probably were. See when we was young we didn't get to town much. We didn't have a car until 1924. So we didn't get to town very much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you visited Studack in the hospital you had a car by that point though.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall when they built the road over Smith Peak from Berry Creek to Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would most people get around before you got cars? How would you travel?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Horse and buggy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall what kinds of crops your parents raised?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, mostly hay. For the horses and the cows. They milked quite a few cows. That is, for them by hand it was quite a few. Back when we went to grade school we probably had as many as 10 or 12 cows. But my sister milked, well my mother milked too for a while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was your whole living made from the farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The whole living on the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a particular type offarm, did you raise particular types of crops?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A little grass seed to sell, very little. And most of the other grains we fed. And we had pigs, chickens, cows, the whole works. In those days most farmers had all of those things. It wasn't specialized like it is now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So most of your neighbors were sustenance farmers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you say "sustenance farmer" back then or would you just say "fanner?"

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We just said farmers then. [In those days there were no taxes, fertilizers were just coming in, no bookkeeping, hardly any chemicals--just fly spray for cows. The only herbicide was a hoe. Education came from experience. Now you have to be an accountant and about everything else just to get by! JRJ
bracketed_corrections: [In those days there were no taxes, fertilizers were just coming in, no bookkeeping, hardly any chemicals--just fly spray for cows. The only herbicide was a hoe. Education came from experience. Now you have to be an accountant and about everything else just to get by! JRJ...]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So f somebody was a fanner then you knew that they had a diverse amount of crops and animals.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did most people have orchards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a small home orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So a home orchard would be one. . . mostly fruit for the family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For the family, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall anybody with commercial orchards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the first commercial orchard I ever knew was Mr. Widmer. He lived near Palestine Hill. And he was an old Swiss bachelor. And he was one of the first ones that had gold delicious apples. He built a little apple storage house. And I know he would give us apples every winter, the smaller and #2 apples which we were tickled to death to get. We had no way to store and keep the apples.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what part of Switzerland this Widmer was from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. I don't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But he was.. . would that be the only other Swiss family in the neighborhood that you can recall then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, right now I can't think of any other Swiss outside the Studacks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall ever seeing any Indian artifacts?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not to amount to anything. I have found some arrowheads myself. I don't even know where they are now, around here somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you find those on this property here, or near Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Most of them I found here, at the back of this farm [His current Peoria road farm along the Willamette river in Linn County], because there used to be an old swamp, kind of a lake bottom there that was drained, before we ever bought the place it was drained. And then I cleared some out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any arrowheads or anything like that near Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall anybody talking about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, as far as you can recall there weren't any Indian signs in that area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I can remember. Of course, in those days I don't think we were very interested in Indian things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any.. . I asked you before f you could recall any stories about Tainpico?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I can't. Only that I heard that it was quite a wild place in the early days. Saloon there, and the stage coaches stopped there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you heard stories about stage coaches. Do you remember any stories about the stage coaches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just that they stopped there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any stories about the saloon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just that there was a saloon there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about stories offights or horse races?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's just what I read.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the stories that you would hear would be more that it was just a wild place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did that mean to you? What did that imply?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I really don't know what to say there. Other than it was just kind of a wild place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear any stories about stage holdups or robberies? Anything to do with gold?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about haunted houses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. When I was a kid I used to think houses were haunted when they'd tell me stories.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any houses in particular that you thought were haunted?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any stories about religious meetings in the Tampico or Soap Creek area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any religious groups in those areas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Green Beriy Smith?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I've heard, or seen his name at times for different things, but I don't remember what it was about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember f you thought he was a good person or a bad person?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Grandma Carter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grandma Carter?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I knew of her, and I probably saw her maybe three or four times. But I knew all of the other Carters, the descendants. There was quite a few of them around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who would be good members of the Carter family to talk to now about the Carter history?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Vincent Carter, and I think he lives in Albany, I believe, and then Lyle Carter is another one, but he lives over in Fstern Oregon someplace, but I'm not just sure what town he lives in. Vincent Carter I think would be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Vincent? Now we talked about Velma Rawie.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, yes. That's right, she would be a good one, a very good one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so she would be kind of like Vincent? You think she might know as much about the Carters as Vincent Carter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think she probably would.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we talked about Coffin Butte. And your family had kind a tradition there. Could you describe that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, when we were kids we used to like to go up on Coffin Butte. In the winter time of course when it snowed we'd go up with our sleds or toboggans, at that time it was a nice smooth surface, before it was all dug up, and it was good sled riding. And kind of a tradition, Easter my parents would invite..

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Tape recorder problem continued.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part II.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: September 30, 1990: Coffin Butte Tour

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following transcript was made from a recorded interview with Jake Rohner that took place during an automobile tour of the Coffin Butte area on September 30, 1990. Stopping points along the tour route are noted on the map at the front of this book with alphabetized letters. The same alphabetic system is used in the following text to coordinate discussions with speqfic locations.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: A. Coffin Butte Landfill

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On top of that little raise right. See that blue roof down in there, or water or whatever it is?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was just this side. . . this was the boundary through here. Of the Schulmerick place and the Steilmacher place. They were both on both sides of the road. In this case the house was on this side and most of the farm land on that side, and the Steilmachers house was down there. Then it run up to our place, and let me see now

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Schulmericics were on the left, or the west side of the road, and the Stellmachers were on the east?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The buildings. But the land was both sides of the road in both cases. We were land locked. We either went to the Tampico Road, because Wiles's was behind us, and the Schulmericks and the Steilmachers was this side. And then the Wiles's were on that side also. Wiles's owned, you can see a little, like a trail up through there? Where most of the trees end? And that was about the boundary between the two Wiles's, see. Walter Wiles was over here to the east and to the north. I think there was 300 or 400 acres or so in that place. And the other one too. See it was divided by the father.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Walter Wiles, he was probably the son of the pioneer, John Wiles? Cause he was the only boy, out of the two families?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know the name of the pioneer Wiles, but he had two sons: Walter and Ed. Ed had one boy, and Walter had one girl. I don't know her name. Ed Wiles, he had just the son, and that was Clarence, and then John was a grandson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then Ed Wiles was probably the son of the original pioneer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and Ed Wiles just about had to be because it was divided between the two, I presume. Unless there was just two brothers came out here and took the donation land claim themselves, you see, but that I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, originally it was just one donation land claim but they had the Hugharts next door that I think they married into.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well, whatever. They always said, well Ed Wiles he lost pert nearly everything he made, inherited, and Walter Wiles made more money. He was a banker, he turned out to be a banker. So their side is wealthy, but the other Wiles used to be. And he lived in town and drove Buicks all the time, and lived in Albany, and was a gentleman farmer you might say, see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he went broke doing it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Practically broke. And he kept selling off pieces. Well he sold to Studacks, he sold to the Mackeys, he sold to my father. And see my father bought everything, that line going up the Butte went straight across up over the Beals Hill, you see. And my father bought 112 acres from Joe Smith on this side of that line, and then later he bought 41 acres from Wiles on the other side. And by that person that originally bought, I think Joe Smith repossessed this piece that my dad bought. I presume he did. Because who ever bought that place, they bought Steilmacher's old house and Steilmacher was gonna build a new house. And the old house was in pretty good shape, it was kind of a rectangular house, nothing fancy. So the people who bought before my father decided to buy Steilmacher's house and move it up there. And the story goes they used four wagons to move it up there, one wagon under each corner. And they cut a swath up through the timber up in there to move it, and why in the hell they moved it clear to the far end of the place, which was that line coming down over the hill when they could have. . . see that oak tree right over, looks like there's a power pole in front of it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This first round oak tree? Well, that was on the Steilmacher's side, and then we had just a few hundred feet on the other side was our north and south line, or our east boundary. Well, and there were some nice trees just the other side of there. And

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: they could have moved the house in there and saved building a road clear to the back end of the farm, you see. But they did. And when Dad bought it was set off of the wagons, it was setting on the ground, but it still was on the two long timbers that went through there when they had bought the place. So he had to put a foundation under it and everything, and they had to build a road up through. Eston Carter owned that place just on the other side, there was about 20 acres in there. He didn't own any of the Butte.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your ownership went back up on the Butte, though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just to the foot of the Butte. It included that round clump of trees right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That oak we're seeing off there just to the northwest there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And our road went in right, can't remember if it was just below those trees or just above those trees. Then Eston Carter's house set up in here. This side a ways from that nice oak tree there, round oak tree. Just this side, it looks like a road in there. Just this side somewhere was his house. So he shared our lane going in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said you were land locked. But you had that road access?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we had that road access. We were landlocked just by the boundaries, but we did have that road access. Then my Dad and Eston Carter we had a rock pit up in there, picked loose with a pick and load it on a wagon and then we would rock the road. And Eston Carter would help us on what he used, and from thereon we had to do it all ourselves.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Before we take off here a second, where that trunk is between towards that blue roof there, we're looking due west, towards the landfill, now that used to be a grove of oaks in there, you say?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh, further up there used to be a grove of oaks. About where that landfill first goes up?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Under that, there was a little. . . we'll go up there pretty quick and see. And that was where our building sat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the ones we can see in the photographs, then. We looked at the photographs of your house up against the base of the hill, and there was some oak trees in through there? That photograph your sister had?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well, yeah, that'd be it then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and thai was the Stelimacher's old house, the one that you lived in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That we lived in, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you said the Beals Hill over here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We always called it the Beals Hill, I don't know whether everybody else did or not. But at least that side, people referred to it as "Beals Hill" And we could see a little bit of a dividing line up through there when we come over in there. Something else you wanted to ask?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah I had a couple of other questions. Now, Carter only owned 20 acres here. How come he only had 20 acres, and how could he make a living off it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was a carpenter. He done carpenter work around the community. And he built houses and things like that on a smaller scale, between farming, see. I never did remember how big his place was, you said it was 20 acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I thought you said it was about 20 acres.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well, yeah, I don't think it was 30, but it was in there somewhere. Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you said you had a rock quarry, up about where they quarried some of the rocks since then. Was that an old. . .? -

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, see that round oak tree. Okay, then see kind of a clay bank in there? Well, right about there was our rock quarry.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Was that in there when you bought the place or did you make that yourself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think we made it ourselves, but I'm not positive. If it was there was very little rock taken out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that's the first time anybody started a quarry on Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it wasn't really a quarry for the public, it was on our own property. And I rather think that my father started that, because as I remember when I first started helping, it was I'd say maybe 50, 100 yards at the most taken out of it. And I know my father took some out before I can remember. And it really wasn't so very big, from where we started the quarry it probably didn't go back over 20 feet or so, maybe 25 at the most, probably not over 50 feet the other way. So you see it wasn't a lot taken out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the first quarry on Coffin Butte, though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was another one toward the other end, that the people at the other end took some out of, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, like the Wiles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the Wiles and the Stambaughs and those used rock out of there. And it wasn't much bigger, it was a little bit bigger than ours.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, then I have two more quick questions. On the landfill there, is that anywhere near what it used to look like? Or are they changing the topography there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, absolutely. See, how it looks by that clump of oak trees?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And, Coffin Butte looked just. . . well, see that first trail that goes around there and the little bit of shrubbery, trees below, and then nothing up there and another little trail?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Coffm Butte looked like that up above all the way down, it came all the way down, and then all at once it started to flatten a little bit. About like where it is just on the other side of those oak trees and to the left. And then it started going up just where that first little tree is on the other side. And this side had a few more trees on the upper level, but not one fourth as many as there are now on the upper level. And there was none on the lower level, where all these quarries are, there was no trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so those trees have kind of grown up and disturbed the quarry area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Disturbed the quarry. And for some reason, well I know one reason, because it wasn't pastured. You see, and those took hold from up above, from seed. Evidently that had blowed over the ridge. There was always a ridge line just like that one on the other side, see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, on the west side there it always looked like that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah, always looked like that. All the way through here, excepting for a few more trees here. Possibly there was just a little more top soil on this part, so maybe they took a little better.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you think about the appearance now. Do you think it's okay because we need landfills or were you kind of sorry that they started changing like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I am sorry they did. But they needed. . . see they used all that rock, this was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: fairly wet ground, and they started building in February, at the worst possible time. And of course they had no time after Pearl Harbor, you see. And so they took this rock out and they come down here and this rock was nearly all taken down here, outside of for the one road up through here. And they would just back those trucks up and put about 3, oh 2 to 3 feet of that rock on, and then they put gravel crushed on top and paved it. And they had quite a few different contractors working at it and one contractor would take out here, and another one there and another one there. And they took out quite a lot on the other end that we can't see from here. And it just kind of defaced it instead of. . . that's where this environmental business would have helped a lot and said, well, take it out in one place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think some of the environmental things that are. . . that's the reason I'm asking these questions, too. You think those environmental concerns or the aesthetic concerns would have been good to have in place at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At that time, yes. I really do. Because there is no reason why they couldn't have started down here at a lower level and just went back. Instead of taking out here, there and everywhere, pock marking it you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the way they're filling in with the landfill now. With the environmental concerns now, and they're still changing the contours.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we gotta have a landfill, I guess. I hate to see it, especially since our homesite's right under it. But eventually I think they will come probably clear down they own all this land, they'll probably come clear down to the highway, you see. And so a lot of that will be years and years to come. They may be all covered back up again, you see, a lot of those scars.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think jf they tried to go to the original contour of the line and just start filling in the scars that would be a better way to do it? Or are they kind of stuck the way the are?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think they're stuck for room the way they are. It wouldn't take long to fill that back up to the original contours. But they could bring it out, well, kind of like it is there on that ridge we see, you know. And then blend it in with the top part that hasn't been disturbed all along here down as far as the highway. And I think in time it would look a lot better.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what you think about it, but that's the way my thinking would be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I think I want your opinion. You grew up here.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: B. Rohner Drive

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's our road, we used to walk to school. It went straight up till it intersected the Butte, and then it went about the same angle as the Butte on back, to our buildings. Then down a little, then downhill just a little bit. Where the buildings were. Went straight across the highway here, and there was .. . it was about, roughly in round figures, it was about a mile up here and a little less than a mile to Wells, but then the school was up the railroad track a ways, so altogether there was about a mile over here and, well 2 miles to school everyday to walk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, this road here, was that in there when you first moved in or did you build that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It might have been in. Eston Carter I think was here a little bit before us, so he probably. . . but as I remember Dad saying the right-of-way belonged to us. With the place. But Eston Carter helped maintain to where his gate was to turn off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now we're looking due west right along...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think due west.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Between a plowed field here and a unattended field. Must be a property line.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yes, this was a plowed field on this side also.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the south side.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On both sides. When we were living here. And Steilmacher on that side and Eston Carter on that side. But of course now it's not being farmed on this side at all. The disposal company owns all this property now over here. From here on. I don't think they own that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were those poplars there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that was all farm land. Those poplars were planted here I'm sure by the State. Because the State owned that for a while and they used the quarry up there for some time. But it seems to me that I have heard that the disposal property bought that from the State, but I'm not sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did they abandon this road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This road here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As soon as Camp Adair bought it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and then they just abandoned the road immediately.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Abandoned the road immediately. Built the other road just south a little bit all the way through.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. Okay. And then the Steilmacher house that you had purchased, did Camp Adair take that house out at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the Steilmacher house came long before. See about, approximately 1915, '16 or so. That it was bought and moved up there. Of course it was never put on it's foundation until my father bought the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so, but then after Camp Adair bought the farm from you, how long did the house stay there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just a short time, and some soldiers were messing around, and it caught on fire and burned down. Not long after Camp Adair.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it kind of upsetting to your family, to see the family home burn like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yes and no. We wanted a new house so bad, and we already had some of the lumber to build a new house, that we didn't care all that much. About the old house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One last question. On the Steilmachers, we never talked about them before. Did they live around here for a lot of years?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I think for a good many years. Because they were older people than my parents. By several years. Quite a few years. And they were here ever since, as long as I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they Swiss?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, German.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had they come straight over from Gennany?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have German accents?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but just Gennan ancesny.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: German ancestry, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he was a gruff man when we were little kids. We were kind of afraid of him because he was gruff and his voice was rather gruff. But they were nice people. Mrs. Steilmacher especially was nice.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have any kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Or yes, yes, they did. They had two, I think two daughters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. They don't live around here anymore or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they're gone, the daughters. They're gone. And the one daughter never had any kids. I don't know about the other one.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: C. Walter Wiles House

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was the Walter Wiles house, the building area was right in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Was this orchard in here at this time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's been here ever since I can remember. There were apple trees in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now let's see, we're on the north side of Coffin Butte. Just on the corner of Highway 99. And then Walter Wiles, he would have been an old timer to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, yes. I never met Walter Wiles. He would have been an old timer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said he had one daughter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As far as I know just one daughter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who purchased this place after he died?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The daughter. I'm pretty sure the daughter did. And they rented to Wes Kester.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. This is where Kester lived.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, this is where Kester lived and he rented since about 1929, I think was when he rented this place and they rented it until Camp Adair took over. And then afterwards Mrs. Walter Wiles I think didn't particularly want it, so Wes Kester had a chance to buy it back. But he decided he didn't want to go in debt that much. And so then I don't remember. I rather think maybe Mrs. Walter Wiles did buy it back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, this place had Coffin Butte. What did they use Coffin Butte for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pasture.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just for pasture?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just for pasture, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then how much of the flat far,nland out here did they have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not positive, but it seems to me like it was around 300 acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now what kind of crops did they raise on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it was mostly like some hay, and vetch, seed, and some ryegrass, and sheep. They had quite a few sheep. And there used to be a barn down towards the other end of the place they called the sheep barn. They didn't grow much grass seeds except ryegrass, back before the war. Except the harding grass which Mr. Stambaugh grew exclusively himself. For seed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when they brought haiiy vetch in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, that was another crop they raised a lot in here. Wes Kester raised. And we raised hairy vetch. So did most of the farmers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when they first brought it in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but I would think it was probably in the late '20's it was first brought in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason everybody started growing it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was profitable. The southern states in different areas used it for a cover crop. Planted for cover crop in their orchards and other things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So about the late 1 920's you think.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, when it first came in. And then it finally faded out, about the time we left here because the weevil got in there, it was similar to the bean weevil. And then the seed wouldn't germinate so you couldn't sell the seed. But now it's making a little comeback again, and of course now they have sprays to eliminate the weevil.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: D. Camp Adair

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was all farmland down here. There was no trees or anything outside of around the buildings. And then when Camp Adair.. . this was all took over, built all barracks and everything down through here. And roads, streets. So there's lots of old foundations in there. It's really not good for anything so the Game Commission owns most of this land down here now. For game, but there's so many rodents in there, possums and stuff, I don't know whether it's much good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're by the historical marker now. Didn't E.E. Wilson have a game ranch out here, even in the old days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not here. Let me see. Oh, it was more, I think there was a game farm at

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Lewisburg. That's the only one I know of, and I don't remember what they called it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so this was Stellmachers back then, back where you were pointing where all the barracks were and then back where the sign for...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Steilmachers and Carters, and Williamson, and oh it took a lot of farms.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One thing we didn't get on the recording that I wanted top on it was all these fields out here, there wasn't any trees to speak of, it was all purple with vetch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you also said that it volunteered, and it was just beautiful because it went up and down the highways. Volunteer vetch.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did the weevil come in and eliminate that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Somewhere I think just prior to when Camp Adair came in in 1942. A few years just prior to that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this whole little basin in here was pretty much, eveiybody was raising vetch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, a lot of people were. Some farmers didn't get into it, they didn't have the right equipment to handle it. But most of them, especially on the lower hilly slopey ground it done very well, where other things wouldn't do as well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did they raise in here before vetch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, some wheat, and some ryegrass. And hay. Of course every farmer used to have some cows, cattle and horses. And they had to raise so much hay to keep the year round. So there was quite a lot of hay raised.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: E. Earth Day Plantation

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We just passed an Earth Day plantation on the left there. What do you think about tree plantations in land like this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it would probably be a good thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about, now we're looking at Christmas tree crops. Can you remember when people started planting those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not exactly, no. But it's been quite a few years now. And I think now it's being over done, for christmas trees. I think a lot of them will end up being forest.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the christmas trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because there's been so much, so many planted that it's like other crops that if the price is good people get into it and pretty soon there's too many of them. So I think quite a lot of these will end of being, you know for lumber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you think about christmas trees as a crop?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's a nice crop to raise. I think it's been a good deal.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever raise any christmas trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. It's just in the last 20. some years that people have been interested in christmas trees. Now, we cleared all this ground. This was our east boundary about where this little trail is across here. And where those big trees are across there was our south boundary and you can see the south boundary up on that ridge. That's what we called Beals Hill over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so that knob up there with the oak is Beals Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, when it all runs into this one, and it might have all been called that I don't really know. But we cleared, it was all in oak timber just like you see up there. Including that ridge that come out there, where the big fir trees are, that was all in oak timber. And then when this place was sold after Camp Adair, people cleared that oak timber off of there and planted fir trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so those are planted fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, those are planted fir.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who planted them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. I don't. Then when the disposal company, now the disposal company owns all of this, you see, and I think they're the ones I think that planted these christmas trees here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The disposal company?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: F. Rohner Farm

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: east boundary. So when did that road come in? Did that maybe have something to do

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: with the christmas trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that's just access to the christmas trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and so when these trees were planted, was that right after Camp Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was a few years until they were planted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And that was the people that bought this land after Camp Adair. Do you recall their name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. I don't. And the garbage, well we called it the garbage company, but it's the disposal company now. They bought part of our old place originally after Camp Adair, because they had the garbage, disposal area started not on our property, beyond our property. And they bought part of it and then later they bought all of it. So they own all of it now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the east side of your boundary there, that'd be Stambaughs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. Stambaughs was way up there on the other side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so, let's see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We're still, we're on our place, but there's the Schulmerick place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Schulmerick.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Schulmerick. And back here is the Steilmacher place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, Schulmerick, that's who I was trying to think of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Our east boundary was Schulmerick and Steilmacher.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and then your south boundary was Beals?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Beals.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All the way across?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All the way from that corner to the other corner.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this is harding grass here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, we're looking at harding grass? As we're just coming into the boundary? That's this taller, tufted grass here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn humrn. But of course here on the shoulder it doesn't grow very tall. We'll see some nice harding grass further back there a ways.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My father had gradually -- every year he hired wood cutters to cut cord wood. This was all oak. And then they used to haul it down to Wells in the fall months. And they'd load it on a freight cars and it was shipped to Portland for fuel. And so little by little. . . and then he had goats, and the goats of course would eat the sprouts and

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: keep them down, and finally the stump would die. And then it would take a few years, several years for the root core to rot out. But he'd get in a hurry so he had this stump puller after they had died, rotted, just enough so the stump puller could pull. We'd work it, every winter we'd work and clear off maybe about 3 or 4 acres of this ground with the stump puller and then farm it. And so all this was once in oak timber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big was the oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I'd say up to about 10 to 12 inches.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was younger oak.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was younger oak, it wasn't the old growth oak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it'd probably seeded in since settlement or something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I would think so, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any of the large old oak trees around through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes there were some. Well, there's one right behind that curve, is quite a large tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now we're looking at a madrone here. Was there very many madrone in the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there wasn't any here on this hill that I can remember, but there was quite a few on the back side of Coffm Butte. On the north side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now, these madrone. Did you call them by another name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we always called them laurel. But they was really madrone. Now here, right out here was our building site.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the north side of the road here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Going back to the douglas-fir earth day plantation sign.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was our building site.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this a hill then before it was cut away?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no. No, this has all been filled in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, isee.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This has all been filled in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it would have been on maybe a level with the road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Well, that's the original level right over there, where that grass is growing. See, the road has been built up some. And this has been built up here too, because

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: they brought top soil out here, excavating for the landfill back there. And then they take of course more top soil off and fill over the landfill, you see. See that's been covered over, you see that slope right through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that hill in front of us that you can see from here have a name? Did you call it anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We always called it the Writsman, or Wiles hill, because Wiles run partway up to about where the trees started, and they farmed right up to the trees, their part of it. And the Writsmans was of course across the road from the end there, kind of. So we just called it the Wiles or Writsman Hill. Supposed to be the Writsman Hill, but who actually owned it I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the little peak in back of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any trees or anything on top of that peak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On back of that hill?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, that was always forest. And a lot of it's been logged off and new growth up there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, how about that hill off there to the southwest. Did that have a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. Not that I know, I'm sure it had a name, but see the Glenders lived on this end of it. And Sulphur Springs Road goes up that side there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did they start calling that Soap Creek Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've heard it Soap Creek Road for a good many years. And Tampico Road, too. I really don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're at the intersection here, the new road that they put in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's where Tampico School used to be. And this is alt new, of course.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, this road here is new too then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. It's new too. This used to all be farm land here and pasture land up there, and we had a trail along, just that we used during the summer. And in the winter if it was dry enough. Right down in that corner, where that little building is right down in that corner, in those trees, that was our boundary with Beals there and Wiles there. And right up where this row of trees is this was our west boundary. It went on up

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: that way quite a ways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you see. . . you could see Glenders' barn real clear then, at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, and the house, and everything. Of course the house isn't there anymore I don't think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, they just took it out a few months ago.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, just a few months ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, 1 took a picture of Gene and his sister on it, and that's the first time they'd been there since 1940. Then they took it out. But could you see any other houses or buildings through here at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's about it. Maybe we could see the Clarence Wiles house, I can't remember clearly, because it was on a knoll. We must have been able to see the Clarence Wiles, or part of it anyway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, that short hill right behind the Glenders, and then there's a hill that's further to the west that's higher. The one that's right behind the house would that be more like Glenders Hill, or would the larger hill up on the back be more of a landmark?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think this was probably called Glenders Hill, this first one here. And I don't know what the other one would have been called.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and Writsman 's Hill, right there, was that commonly called Writsman 'S Hill, or was that just your family that maybe called it that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, our family mainly that called it that. I don't remember anybody calling it Writsman Hill or any other name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so these names that we're kind of attaching to things, it would just be the local family would use it for reference.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you went to Tampico School there -- did you go to Tampico School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no, I went to Wellsdale.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, that was before Tampico.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that was before Tampico. I can't remember, but it seemed to me like I was maybe in the second grade or so, maybe the third, when they built Tampico school. I can just faintly remember them building Tampico School. Because we had some good friends, a boy older than I and a boy just younger and they went to Tampico School.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How come you didn't? That was a lot closer, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was no road to it. No road. You'd have to walk across the fields to get to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any creeks in through this area that had a name other than Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just Berry Creek is all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I saw a reference where they said, and I think they made a mistake, but they said Glenders Creek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's possible there could have been Glenders Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not that you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I recall, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I have heard people other than your family refer to that hill up there as Writsman 'S Hill, but never Wiles Hill. Can you recall evely hearing any other family call that Writsmans Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not really.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Beals Hill? Could you recall any other family calling it by that name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't defmitely, but it seems like I have heard it called Beals Hill by other people but I can't say for sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and how about Glenders Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I've heard that called Glenders Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, can you think of anything else in this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Were there more than one Writsman?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, Frances Writsman was the house you were born in, and Alfred Writsman lived down at the other end of the valley. Writsmans Creek is down there, and what they call Baker Mountain now. Used to be called Writsmans Peak.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Quite a little further south?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Towards Sulphur Springs, yeah. No, west towards Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, west toward Sulphur Springs. Oh, I didn't know there was another Writsman.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, there's still Writsmans Creek back there. Now they say "Writzmans" [RITZ-munz]. So those are the types of things we're trying to correct here. [Correct pronunciation is RITES-

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: munz. BZ] ***

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One more question before we leave. We've got quite a bit of trees and it looks like some volunteer [crab] apple and pine. Were any of these trees here back then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. When my father came here. . . see, we're on the 41 acres that my father bought from Ed Wiles. It run up to the base of Beals Hill there. And like I say, the corner was down in there, see. It's a square corner, and it run up over the hill. Well you can see the line there, see the tall trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, it's right between the christmas trees and the oak trees on Beals Hill there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that was our line. And then the 41 acres run right to the base of the hill where it started to go up. The north-south line, and went up over Coffm Butte, you know that line I showed you there at Coffin Butte. So this was 41 acres here. And there was no fence row here at all because he bought that from Wiles, so they cut it off there, you see there was no fence row.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that fence row there was one that you constructed after you bought it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. We put in a line fence and while we were here, until 1942, there was nothing growing there, we kept it clean, excepting where that grove of ash trees is, that was always there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh that grove was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that grove was there. But none of these this way. But now since they've abandoned farming, why, and those, I would say nearly all of those are thornberries, wild thornberries or wild hawthorn I think they call it. And you know the birds eat the seeds and they sit on a fence post and then a tree starts you see. But there was between the 41 acres and the 112 that my father bought from Joe Smith, there was a line through there, and it was all thornberries like that, bigger, and my father cleared that out by hand.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody call it hawthorn back in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we just called it thorn trees. They've got thorns nearly an inch long. Miserable things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about on the madrone, did anybody say madrone back in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I can remember. Not that I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about on the big oak trees, did you call them any kind of oak. Did you say "white oak," or "Oregon oak"?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, fact is we called it "grub oak."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Grub oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grub. Most of the farmers did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that even mean the big old growth oak trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We just called them all just grub oak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. On Writsman,s Hill up there, did that have trees on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but it's got more trees than it used to have.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have any prairie ground down lower, or any pasture ground?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it had some pasture ground. The Wiles farmed it up to where it started to go up a little steeper, that was their boundary, and then there was open ground above that a ways. A lot of the. . . they used to pasture all those hills, sheep and cattle and one thing and another, and of course that discouraged new seeding. Well, it would seed, but they'd eat the little plants off. Since they don't pasture this ground any more why the trees have come in. Took root.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the trees that came into that pasture ground that was above Wiles. Wio used that pasture ground?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know who owned it, who used it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We used to go, when we were kids, we used to go up there and pick strawberries, wild strawberries, quite a bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, on that hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any wildflowers up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I really can't. But I'm sure there was plenty of wildflowers up there. We didn't ever go up there to. . . only reason we went up there was at strawberry time to pick strawberries. Where up here, we'd go up here for playing around, and we'd pick wildflowers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Coffin Butte.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On Coffin Butte.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any names of wildflowers on here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, spring beauties and ladyslippers. And there was another kind, just some, we just called them something and I don't remember now what, we didn't know the name. And of course the dogwoods. Which we picked every Easter usually.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so when you had your Easter celebrations up here on Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we wouldn't really have the celebration here. We'd have the dinner and stuff and everything at home there, and then us kids would go up on the Butte. And pick some flowers and things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the dogwoods you kind of associated with Easter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you give any kind of religious sign jficance to the dogwoods?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. It's just that it was about that time they were in bloom. Some years they were further along than others, because Easter varies, but it was just about that time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One more question on Writsmans Hill there. Between that and the larger hill in the background, there's kind of a long bench. Do you remember any trails up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Remember any stories about Indians having anything to do with up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. We used to go up there and cut our christmas tree up there a lot of different times.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Writsmans Hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it younger trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, younger trees.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: G. Soap Creek Bridge

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, this was farmed for a ways down there, and then down toward that end and up that side was pretty marshy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Whose marsh was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wiles, Clarence Wiles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have a name for it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No slough, or marsh, or anything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no name for it. That I know of anyway. Yeah, now there used to be a pit right in this area where the neighbors up in here used to take rock out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this pit on. . . lets see, we're on the west end of Coffin Butte. This would be Wiles would use.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Ed Wiles end of the Butte, yeah. Ed Wiles would use it and the Stambaughs and the Mackeys and different ones around here would use it. I think they were just, I don't think they had to pay anything for the rock they got out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this in here, did they have hairy vetch growing up through this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the whole basin out through here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. You could see it from here, even as far as Portland you'd see hairy vetch. And we used to have a, right at the base of the Butte here on around here, sort of used to have our summer trail through here where we'd drive when it wasn't too wet, we'd drive up here to the Stambaughs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there's an old road in through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, just a farmer trail through the Wiles place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now we're approaching the bridge here to Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is Soap Creek. The Army engineers put this bridge in. The original bridge was further down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, how far down was it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I'll show you pretty quick. See this was all, in here was just like this. Trees and brushes through here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now lets see, we're at the intersection of, well it says Rifle Range, and Wiles Road. Was that called Wiles Road back in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, well I'm pretty sure it was called Wiles Road back in those days. Now that road was in, ever since I can remember, that was the boundary between Stambaugh and Wiles. This was all Stambaugh over here. And of course this was all trees and brush in here. And this is the original bridge area here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So we're turning due east and we're crossing Soap Creek again?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we're turning more north, northeast a little bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And now there's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And now, let's see, yeah we would come right through this area in here. This has been built up a little bit in here. We would come through this area and open the gate here and then we could go to the Mackeys or Stambaughs here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So f you went to the Stambaughs you had to cross a bridge right about in this area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but if we went to the Mackeys we didn't have to cross. Yeah, I'd say it was within 100 feet or so of where it is now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you say it was upstream or downstream?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it went more straight across to a bend, straight across, and then bent again. No, I believe that's about the original road up in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where the road is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where it is now, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay, and this went out to the Mackeys.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To the Mackeys, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long had they lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't. . . lets see, 19. . , oh, '20-'24 in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall who they bought from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wiles. Ed Wiles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the properly on the other side of theirs, was that Wiles, or did that go out to Carters?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Other side of the road you mean?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, on the other side of Mackeys.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, Ed Wiles went down there about another mile, to the boundary, to that road that goes east and west.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was trying to figure out where. . . the brush has grown up so much in here. I think the bridge might have been this way a little bit. Then we kind of went across like that and then swung back a little bit.
