entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So we're looking at this brown house here between the two Soap Creek bridges that we just crossed. And you think the bridge might have been back of that maybe somewhere?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I would say somewhere between the end of the house and the end of the bridge,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: right in there somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: H. Stambaugh Lane

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If I could find the Stambaugh lane here, I could tell better, but it's all grown up so much. It really has grown up. As I remember it, it was pretty clear going back in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It just about had to be further down here, because there's a big oak tree that was. the house went back in there, there was brush just like those ash there and stuff behind, and then on that side there was all, there was about a 4-acre field in there. I see a big oak tree, it must have been down here a little bit further then. Then there was brush along the creek. Here, by golly, yeah, there's the field so the Stambaugh house was right back in there. So, that's pretty close to where the bridge used to be. Because I know after we went through the gate we come this way a little ways and went in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kinds of crops did the Mackeys raise?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they had some cows and some horses, and they raised hay. Here we can see better. That was the field there, and then the house was up against those trees over in there and the barn was down toward the other end of the field.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So where those blackberries are? We're looking at a little opening, could that have been the Stainbaugh lane? This little opening?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, this must have been the Stambaugh lane and that bridge must be darn near to where it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it pointed in the same direction, too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was more of an angle, it went more straight across.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they ever have any trouble with flooding in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any geese or duck migrations through this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, every year they migrate one way or the other. Through this area. I think more or less clear across the valley. Yeah, they haven't any of them that I know of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: migrated south yet, but pretty soon we'll be hearing them.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: I. Mackey Orchard

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: These filberts that are through here, were those here back in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they. . . no, that . . . well yes, yes, they were planted by the Armstrongs. That later bought the Mackey place. And I see there is a house back down in there now. I didn't know it was there. Now the Armstrongs, or the Mackeys built a house right in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, is that an old walnut tree there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's a walnut tree, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So these apples here, are those just seedlings along the fence row?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think possibly they're seedlings, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So is that remnants of an old orchard back there off to the left there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be the Mackey orchard or the Annstrong orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the Mackey's probably, those. And the house was right in here somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the Mackeys built that house. There wasn't any house before then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they bought the bare land. Just like the Studacks and my father, the 41 acres, it was all bare land. See they, cause Ed evidently could use a little more money of something, why he'd sell a piece of ground. And the Mackeys owned this knoll here on the other side also. Then of course when Camp Adair came in Wiles still owned this hill here and this side here and that side down through that east-west road down there just the other side of those trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, that east-west road. I'm not familiar with that. Is that the one that goes out to Suver Junction, and out to Berry Creek? Does it have a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it don't have a name that I can remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who had the land on the other side of the road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the other side of the road? Walter Wiles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so it'd be Walter Wiles, and then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Walter Wiles had this, and all that was on the other side of the road. It went back up this way a little ways. Probably as far as the Ed Wiles place went. And of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: course this road, Camp Adair built this road in through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the road along what would be the northeast face of Coffin Butte was built by Camp Adair.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was built by Camp Adair, yes. They had some, I think some pistol ranges and things along in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did the neighbors think about Adair moving in and moving evetybody out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they didn't like it. Most of them didn't like it very well. Most of them were old timers and still original inherited, donation. . . or parts of donation land claims you see. And I know we hated terribly to move. And of course we were newcomers more or less to the area. And we had just gotten the place fixed up to the way father wanted it, except for the house. That was the next year's project, was to build a new house. We had a new barn in 1937 and in 1941 we built the new barn and had it almost done except for the siding on two sides. And when they took over, so we hated terribly to leave the place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: you don't have to take it, but you can take it to court. But it will be in the courts for maybe two or three years, until it gets settled. Well, in our case and in a lot of other cases, they couldn't stand that you see, because they had to have a place to go to because of the cattle and one thing and another. But what they failed to tell us was that, later on we found this out, that they paid you a lot of the money anyway, right to start with, and if you won in court you got more money. And if you didn't win why it would cost you the court cost, but you'd get the rest of the money. And that they failed to tell you, they said well, you just won't get any money. See, there was kind of crookedness on the part of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the people that were negotiating for the government, were those like real estate dealers, or were they hired by the Army?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really don't know. I know I sure I didn't like that one man that was negotiating with us. He was kind of a bully. He said, "Well, it's too damn bad. You'll just have to take it to court, and maybe it'll be a couple years till it gets settled."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he the same one that negotiated with the other families here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That I don't know, but he negotiated with a lot of them right at first because it was real urgent that they get started on it, so all that was in the building area they

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: negotiated with right away, you see. But those outside, they had more time to think about it and. Well, Beals was one of them took them to court, and I know several others did fmally. Well, they could afford it you see, they had money. In the case of Beals, they had another farm to go to in Linn County. So they weren't put out all that much if they had to wait. But they had won a larger settlement. And we could have too, if they had told us that we get most of the money down anyway and we just have to wait on the rest of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that one guy that caine in, was he from Oregon or did they send him out

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: from

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Washington, DC?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea where he was from.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pretty pushy.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty pushy, yeah, big husky bully sort of a guy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember his name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I wish I would have kept it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you said that a lot of the Donation Land Claim people had been here since the beginning, and then you said you were the newcomer, you'd only been here for 20 or 30 years. Was there kind of, in the neighborhood, was there kind of a dj(ference between the Wiles, and maybe the Glenders and Marcks who'd been here a little bit longer, and Schulmericics and Rohners, all those people, were they kind of stratified by how long they'd been here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't believe so. Didn't have that feeling, anyway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was all just community pretty much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Community, pretty much. And, well, World War I they were a little bit more bitter about the German speaking people. And I don't blame them. Because that was World War I.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they d{fferenticue between you Swiss and the Germans?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, most of them did, most of them did I'm sure. And we certainly didn't speak German. Our native language amongst other people that were English speaking. And of course our German, well my father and mother, they could talk the regular high German, but all of us kids why we knew only the dialect, which was German, but the regular German could hardly understand.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could your parents speak English?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, my father could fairly well because he spent about 5 years in Kansas My mother came fresh from Switzerland. And at home we always talked in the Swiss dialect, which I'm glad we did because it's stayed with me better in later years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said when you started school you couldn't speak any English.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, just once in a while a word that I'd picked up from a hired man. I heard some wood cutters, and picked up words here and there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember what kind of words those were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said right around World War I, there was problems with people speaking Gennan speaking dialects, and you were starting school, and you had to have a German speaking dialect -- did you have any problems?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not that I remember in school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, in World War ii, all the neighbors were being forced to move. Were you all kind of in a group together, feel equally put upon, or did dWerem neighbors kind of react different to it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there was neighbors that acted different. Some of them, well it was a good chance to sell the farm. Others of course were old timers, they dreaded the move. I was really an old timer, because even though I'm Swiss I was born here, and I can't remember any other home, except our farm. I don't even remember the Writsman place as far as memories except what my parents talked about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your whole life you'd been here, from the day you were born?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, my whole life had been here, really. And I was born here. Switzerland is a beautiful country, but there is a lot more opportunity here, back in the earlier days anyway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: i'm curious, this is kind of a little bit off the topic, but you were born here and now we're doing a history here. Do you think that's generally a good idea?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I imagine it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I know you are being real cooperative. But I don't know f you are cooperating just to kind of be nice to me or you think it's an important thing that we understand these situations.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think it's important that we understand this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of use can you see being made of a history like this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really don't know.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Came to my mind just minutes ago sitting there, that I believe I have seen more deer since we've lived where we are now, than I have all the time I was near Camp Adair. We had quite a few deer in the river bottoms, and I see deer quite often, where here we rarely ever saw a deer cross our farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you think in terms of hunting it f you did see it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you think in terms of going and shooting a deer f it'd cross your farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I've never been a hunter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about fishing through here. Did you ever fish on Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, mostly crawdad catching.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. How about swimming. Did you have a swimming hole through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Well, I never did really learn how to swim, and there weren't very many swimming holes here on Soap Creek, but we did lots of wading around Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about, were there a lot ofpheasants in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there were a lot of pheasants. Dad used to raise corn for the hogs, ear corn, and there were a lot of pheasants in the corn field in the late fall. And he'd go out, and corn wouldn't keep on the cob very good in this part of the country. Now they can dry it, but in those days it didn't keep good, so he'd leave it on the stalk and go out in the sled in the winter time and pick a bunch for a week or so supply and feed the hogs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there wild game birds and grouse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, there were grouse. On Coffin Butte, Beals Hill, there were grouse. One day I got in the dog house with mom, I don't remember what I did. So I went up on Beals Hill and I scared up a grouse. And it took off and hit the woven wire fence and knocked itself cuckoo. So I went up and grabbed him and wrung his neck, brought him home, so I was OK then, I got out of the dog house. Yeah, we used to hunt gray squirrels. I said I'm not much of a hunter, when I was a kid I did. Well, let's stop here for a minute, I want to look at something. You can shut that off if you

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: want to.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: J. Harding Grass Field

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: North/south boundary between the Writsman place and Stambaugh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This field here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This field. Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where that vegetation line is there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The vegetation line is more or less the boundary. Well, where the trees are, and a little of that vegetation there was on Stambaugh's side. Where those further trees are. And that's where he raised his harding grass and he liked this very much because it was protected by trees. Pretty well all the way around. There used to be quite a few trees over in here. And it liked the stuff when it got ripe to whip those heads around because the seed would fall out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the harding grass was in this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All this cultivated ground here was in harding grass.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many acres is that about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think possibly he had 60, maybe 80 acres. I doubt it was 80, but it's somewhere along in there. That's what we used to bind at night. Now down, I was going to show you that, now there is some harding grass, some taller stuff down in there. That's where we got that bouquet that she's got in on the dining room table.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did Stambaugh start raising harding grass here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, ever since I can remember. Yeah, just about ever since I can remember. He started on smaller scale and then about 1920, '29 and '30. He did raise some flax for linen for the State Penitentiary. Well, we did, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I wanted to ask you quite a bit about the harding grass because eveiybody mentions it. Is this a good place or should we maybe wait till a little bit later and then go into it in detail like the other night.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we can wait till a little later. We should be home. I think we probably should be home.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: K. Applegate Trail

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, well see Wiles is.. . they farmed that, that's farm land. And that was about their border.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Up on the other side there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That side of the field was their border, through there, more or less. Between the hill property, and I don't know who owned the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now there's an orchard up there, we can see it. You said there used to be a lot of wild pears around. But there's some apples up in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, wild apples, used to be a lot of apples too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And there is some sites of some old buildings up in that area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, there is? I can't remember them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You can't remember anything up there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And there is some old. . . there is an old road and trail along right between the edge of the cultivation and that brush there. Can you remember anything about an old road through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, only thing I can figure is maybe they took wood out of the place there. Or maybe a few logs at one time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, we're going along Tampico Road and we're coming right into the north face of Writsman 's Hill. And on the left, on the west side there's a strip of vegetation. Do you recall anything around that vegetation through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. See now the Writsman place joined the Stambaugh place down there where we stopped, you know. And there used to be - there was been some cleared so there was more uncleared land down just east of us here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now this out through here was haiiy vetch fields?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, hairy vetch. At one time when Dobrinin owned the place and I worked for him and he had a pretty large field of buckwheat down in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This side there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now on this corner there is a concrete plate. We're right at the gate. And it goes along the base of Writsman 's Hill along the south side. Do you remember any structures or anything

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: through this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's a couple big pear trees there. Can you remember anything about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I rather suspect the pear trees were wild because there were lots of wild pear trees around here. Lots of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: L. Writsman Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Put in up here. And some of them are still in use down at the far end, but these have all, a lot of them have been filled back in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the rifle ranges came all the way up to the road here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just almost to the road, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this road about the same place in those days as it is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, same place. It's wider now. That's a new orchard and that house that I never knew was in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Whose place was this in through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Writsman.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they call it the Dobrinin place after Dobrinin got it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They didn't call it the Writsman 's place anymore.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Well, some old timers might have, but the newer people they called it Dobrinins. Now as I remember, just where that house.. . I think they've maybe, they've widened this road and possibly straightened it just a little bit. I think maybe it made a little more of a bend like that. I think that house had to be pretty close up in here someplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Writsman 'S house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cause we took the picture in front and back there it all slopes down too fast, too

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: steep. And I think it was pretty close right up in here and the barn was down that way. Closer toward that brush. As I remember there was quite a little distance between the barn and the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The house, but it/aced off toward Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the house faced here, and the picture, or that drawing, was taken at Coffm Butte.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the drawing was made up here further? Could we go up there and maybe take a photograph of where you think the drawing was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now do you recall anything on the left hand side of the road, on the west in through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There is some old orchard in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is there? It would almost be possible that the house was on this. Because I think that drawing shows the road maybe bending a little bit in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have a name for that hill up in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear it called a name since then? Smith Peak or Smith Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now there's a little creek that comes back in here. Did that creek have a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know but what the house could have been up in here. [Walking around]. Right in here somewhere there was a boundary between the Writsman place and, well, we called it the Sheppard place, but I don't know who was there when my parents lived here, that is, who owned that place. But in the later years when I was a young fellow I remember the Sheppards living there. And, well, now, prior to that there was somebody else lived there too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Before the Sheppards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Before the Sheppards. Wauble was her name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wauble?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn hmm, Wauble.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how that's spelled?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. Can't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've never heard that name before. Do you remember any stories about her?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bia just heard that the Sheppards bought from Mrs. Wauble?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No husband.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, there was a Mr. and Mrs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, the Waublefainily.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Wauble family. And they had, I believe they had one son. I'm pretty sure they had one son.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know anything about the Sheppard's logging?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, on that hill there. That's all in firs now, and there is oak on top. Can you remember how that used to look?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember seeing hardly any firs on that place. And Mr. Stambaugh rented that place. Must have, from the Sheppards. Because after Camp Adair came in we were, we harvested it for one or two years, after that. They let us come in and harvest it. We were kind of concerned, they were using the rifle range dawn there, and it was pointed up towards that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now when Dobrinin . . . now we're standing on basically your birthplace here. The old Writsman homestead place. Now Dobrinins when they bought it they lived in this house and it burned down.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it burned down. I think they lived in it a few years and it burned down and then they built a newer house further down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe where the yellow house is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this side a ways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. What kind of house did they build?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember now, not even what it looked like. All I can remember is they built a newer house. I do faintly remember there was a. . . I faintly remember and I'm pretty sure there was an old kind of a log type house there at one time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember that log house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Writsman house was here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the log house was here when the Writsman 's house was here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember where that log house was located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Down that way a ways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Towards maybe where the red shed is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, approximately, it was back a ways from the road. It was more down where it got a little more level.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a road anywhere through this area heading towards Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was the only road here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, there was no road going off this one?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So we had Sheppards, Dobrinins, Stambaughs, Clarence Wiles.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn hmm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And do you know what happened to that log house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. I don't remember if it burned down or they tore it down. I just can't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And then the barn was located...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Down toward the creek there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From the yellow house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Not too awful far from this house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there an orchard through this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I believe there were some big trees down in there. Old fruit trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. How about this road here off to the north here. Anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember. It just wasn't very far, it might have been pretty close to the Sheppard boundary.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever find that log house? Or you remember anything about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember nothing at this place. I don't know how long my father and mother were here, whether they were here just three years, or whether they were here four

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: years. Possibly five, maybe. Well, they moved here before I was born, and I was born in February. And truthfully, I can't really remember anything before 1st grade.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now the log house, was that there after this house burned doz?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it was there. Wait a minute. That I couldn't say. I do remember that log house being there, I do believe it was. Dobrinins built another house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they built their house a little closer to where the log house was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, a little closer to the log house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you can't remember anything about this while you lived here. Do you remember anything about the Dobrinins while they were here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yes I used to work for them quite a lot. Every harvest, and in between, I'd walk across the pasture, to my place down there. I was tickled to death to have a job in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have any special meaning because you were born here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not really because I don't remember it! I don't remember the place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bucking hay on the old birth place didn't make any special difference to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, in those days it didn't mean anything. Now it means more. I wish I'd paid more attention and tried to remember things like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is this a creek back here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it's a little creek. I don't know if it runs all summer or not, I can't remember that. I really kind of think maybe a little trickle runs through there in the summer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you just call that a branch of Soap Creek or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yes, because I know no other name for it. It's possible it has another name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there anything else through this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, there's some big walnut. I almost suspect . . . you see there was a driveway into the barn quite a ways this side of the house. And it must have run right along in here because there's bank most of the way in. And I bet that log house sat right out in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In those remnants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now did those walnuts. . . were they here when, can you remember them from the Dobrinins or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I remember trees being around that old log house, but I don't recollect what they were. Well, they almost had to be walnuts because I recollect them being fairly large trees. I just wouldn't be a bit surprised if it was right in here where that log house was. I know the log house was quite a little distance from the other house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you don't remember anything in particular about these walnuts or anything, other than that there were trees around the log house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mike had quite a family. He was Russian. And I think he was kind of southern part of Russia, and he must have been a little bit Jewish because he wouldn't eat pork. And he was a little wiry fellow and his wife was a little larger, husky, and Mike thought the world of me. You're not recording, are you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh yes, I'd like to. You want me to turn it off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well, no that's all right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is the only stomy we've got on the Dobrinins.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And he used to think the world of me. He'd take me places like when he'd go to Tillamook and buy some calves, dairy calves, and raise them, and he'd take me with him. And one time we went up to Washington, I can't remember for sure. . . I should pay attention to who the hell is behind me [car approaches from rear] . . . I can't remember for sure why we went up there but he took me along. And he, always when he. . . well, like when we were over in Tillamook, anyway, he'd see a big husky young gal my age you know, he always thought I oughta get married, you see I was single until I was 42, and he says "Oh, you better get acquainted with her and marry her. She's a big husky gal, she could do a lot of farm work."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he serious?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, he was serious. He was serious. But I worked for him a lot, every year. Now and then I'd work for during school. And usually during harvest I'd run the combine when he'd run header from the tractor, the lowering and raising of the header, and the daughter, she was a little younger than I, she'd done the sack sewing,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and when he got his done, he'd do custom work for other farmers. And her name was Agnes. She was a nice gal, nice looking gal, hard working gal. Now, you can shut it off. [Tells storyj

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: M. Studack Farm

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This ash swale belonged to the Glenders. Fact is, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, I've got this going again here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think the largest part did. And..

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there trees in here in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there was ash trees in there. Now right in here. I don't think Studack owned any of the ash swale. Yeah, that must have been their line fence right here. Yeah, that was there. Then Glenders started in. And all this farm land here was Studacks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would they do with this land?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they had some cows. They raised hay on it and grass, and things like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now Studacks bought this land from

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: From Wiles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now there's some trees in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the building area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, there's a plum orchard in there or something. Did Studack plant that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It could have been somebody after Studack planted the plums. I really don't know. See Studack originally bought it and then he was killed in 1928, later Albert Zundt bought it. And I think that might have been the driveway right there, goes back in and the house. No, wait a minute, the house was on that side. Right back in here is where the house was somewhere. Yeah, the house was right back in here, because we're pretty close to the creek, there's the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have any trouble with flooding?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything about the creek in through here. Like an old swimming hole or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we've waded all through and up that way quite a ways, and down below Starnbaughs and back at Mackeys. And over in here was a big old barn. And we

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: tore that barn down, after Camp Adair took it over. And see my uncle owned the place at the time Camp Adair took it over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who was your uncle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oswald Rohner.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: N. Clarence Wiles Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: '43 it think it was, when we built our barn, or '44 maybe. And we built it all out of lumber taken out of that old barn and Stambaugh's barn, and some sheds that Stambaugh had because we couldn't buy new lumber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, in the '40's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, in the '40's. Here's Clarence Wiles' place. Probably the original driveway right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right where it's at now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where it's at now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything in particular about this house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a nice house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nice house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nice house. Fact is, that all the windows. . . you know where my nephew is, where the warehouse, the Rohner warehouse?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well you pointed it out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we tore this house down, and nearly all the lumber in that house came out of this house. This was a huge house. And we tore down and the joists in this house were about 30 feet or longer. And we couldn't haul it on a farm truck so we had to pile it up here. And we finally managed to find a truck. Not too long, just a matter of days, we found a truck that could haul that. We come out here to get it it was gone. And so we found out later that the Army engineers, or not the Army engineers, the Army. . . the upper, you know what I mean, that gets to tell the little guy what to do, they said to go out there was a lot of mud down there around the buildings. They didn't have any sidewalks. They said go out and rustle some old lumber and build sidewalks around here to keep out of the mud. So they sent the soldiers out here and then they found this pile of lumber up here and so they took it

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and sawed it up in short pieces and made planks out of it. So we complained at what happened. So by God we got a priority to buy some new lumber then to buy some new lumber then to replace those joists so we could go ahead and build the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember a windmill up here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, yes, I remember the windmill. And I don't remember exactly when the house was built but it was built right about World War I time. Maybe, right after I think. And the house sit up here on top of this knoll.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there an older house here before then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, evidently. I don't remember the older house. Evidently there was an older house. Well it's too messy down in here to go down in here. And then as we go down the knoll there then the barn, the dairy barn was down about where those trees are down just off to the left.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's a bunch of St. Johns Wort out here to our left. Was that somewhere around where the front yard was maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, now, let me think now. The house was right up in there, and I think these maple trees was on this side of the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were planted, maybe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It could be they were planted. Yeah, because we could see the house plainly from the Butte there, from that side. There was an old cherry tree in there, just the west side of the house. Had big, black beautiful cherries and they used to give us the cherries, what was left. And when we were kids we'd go up across the pasture with the buckets, to get cherries. To eat and can.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that tree still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. It may be there yet. It's possible it could have died. Just shut it off for a minute. fl'ells story]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: These fields were Clarence Wiles' here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This one here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This little field in here, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're just looking at the one on the north side of Soap Creek on the east side of Tampico Road, the little field that's just been plowed here recently.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then here's the Studacks.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Here's the Studacks, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember an old bridge or a little foot path?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was a bridge across there. There was a bridge across there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this kind of marshy in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not where these trees are. They wouldn't grow if it was marshy. Except ash, ash will grow. But there are some other trees in there. Then it starts getting, you wouldn't call it marshy, but it starts getting a little wetter ground out here. And the closer to that, back there it was a little there too, but the closer to this ash swale the wetter the ground got. Now that ash swale all through there is considered marshy more or less.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where this 4 is, and there is a gate there, it's the fourth stop on that [Historic Soap Creek Auto] tour. Can you remember any old road or anything going out through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Through there? No, no there was never a road through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And where the Studacks were, did they build their house, was there ever a house there before?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they just bought the bare land from Wiles. And then they built the house and the barn, same way the Mackeys, it was bare land.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and where Wiles had that big old barn there, did they buy that barn too, or did Wiles keep that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wiles kept that on the other side of the creek. He just sold what was on this side of the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And did you get like a contract from the Anny to tear the Wiles barn down and to tear the house down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, the owners had a chance to buy their buildings back if they wanted to buy them back. For a small fee. And so my uncle bought that barn and the house back for us to tear down, because we knew we couldn't buy new lumber during the war, and we had to build over there because there wasn't a barn fit for milking 20 cows that we had, Of course there was the priority and I got deferred until we could build a barn. So, for the last time, they said, well the barn done or not done this is the last deferral

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: you're gonna get from us. So we hurried up and then in the meantime they came up things were going a little better and they wouldn't draft anybody over 28 anymore and I was over 28.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so you got lucky.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: O. Roy Barzee House

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Got lucky, yeah. Yeah, this is the Sulphur Springs Road here. I guess Tampico school was right down in there somewhere. Beals' house was, well we kinda drove in down below and then across, it was down in here and then the Glenders was, that's their barn, yeah, I believe the house was about in there. Yeah, I think that's where. the road to the right to the barn. And this is I think where the Barzees had a house. This was Lester Barzee on this side and then, wait a minute not Lester, I can't think of his name. Lester was on the highway side. Isn't it awful, sometimes I can't recall my best friend's name. Till all at once it comes to me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why I was curious, because on the Barzees, I thought the Barzees lived here but you pointed out the other side of the road, and 1 thought well that's something new. But there's two brothers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's two brothers, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. Where did Oswald Rohner live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Clarence Wiles' house. See he bought that when he came out from Kansas, he bought that house and farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let me think. Wait a minute, I said that was the driveway. This was the Barzee's driveway here. And that road of course wasn't in. How far it went that way I don't know, but anyway the two places met back in there somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is Brenneman 's now. Do you know Brenneman?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But this was the Barzee place up until Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And.. . that's new in here, I've never seen that before. Well I haven't been up this road for a long time. I think the Barzees joined the Blakes down there but I'm not sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Well, the Hoffinans were in here somewhere.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I was just gonna say, now Grover Hoffman lived back up in here somewhere. Probably right about where those. . . here somewhere, yeah. See, this used to be the main road straight through here. And this has only been here since Camp Adair. Do you want to go through the old road?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, it doesn't go all the way through, but.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Don't it go all the way through?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not anymore. They blocked it off

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they blocked it? The hell they did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But this would go straight through to the Blakes though, right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then this loop in here they built since Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, since Adair.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there would have been Blake, Hoffman, Barzee, Beals, Glenders,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the other side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I can't remember anybody else but Hoffman's on this side. And I don't think he had too big a place. He might have went clear to Glenders, I don't know. Unless it was, somebody owned some land in there without buildings. There was no buildings.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Between Hoffinans and Glenders.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And, turn that thing off a minute will you? [Tells story]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're talking about Roy Barzee now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, his name was Roy Barzee, and he had two daughters and a son. Arnold Barzee. He lives at. . . he has an apartment or whatever you call it, an apartment at the Mennonite home, you home. If you'd ever want to talk to him he could tell you a lot about Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, now there is something that I'd like to ask you about. You mentioned the Kilmers before, and people told me that there had been a Mennonite settlement in the Beny Creek area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There were several back there. Kilmers and I think another name I told you, but I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: can't remember it off hand. Shank.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Shank?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Shank, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They were Mennonites, too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And were the Barzees part of that then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no, no, no, the Barzees weren't Mennonite, they just. . lots of people go to the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mennonite home from other religions.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. Do you remember any stories about the Mennonite community or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. All I can remember is hearing my mother tell about visiting back and forth some when we lived on the Writsman place, with the Kilmers and the Shanks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1 see. Were there anything different about the Mennonites, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, mighty fine people. And now in later years I've had a lot of contact with Mennonite people south of us on Peoria Road. Some of the finest people I've ever known. They're honest and industrious, I'd trust a Mennonite for a long, long ways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know why they lived in a community there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't really. But they do, pretty much so. Because south of Peoria a ways there is an old community. They have their own school, grade school there. And there are a lot of farmers right in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there more families, did you ever hear of, than like the Kilmers and Shanks, or could that have been the whole community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's all I can remember. I'm sure there might have been more in that area. I think there are quite a few in other areas. . . around Sheridan I believe there are quite a few. Fact is, I think some of those people from that area went later to Sheridan.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Kilmers and the Shanks may have moved to Sheridan?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's kind of what I remember, but I'm not positive that they went to Sheridan.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know why they moved out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now there is also talk when Adair came in that they dug up a lot of the family cemeteries, pioneer cemeteries.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They did. They did, and they relocated them I think to. . . If I remember right to the cemetery just south of Monmouth. Along 99.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason they did that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they were using artillery shells in the area. And I suppose to keep from shooting up the cemeteries. And they moved the bodies.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that upset any of the local families?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I didn't have any contact with any of the families that were concerned, so I really don't know. I suppose it probably upset some of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There is a pioneer cemetery on Berry Creek where some Kilmer children were buried. And there is some dispute whether they dug up that cemetery or not. Did you ever hear of any of the cemeteries not getting dug up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So as far as you know they moved everybody?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They moved everybody. Well, there was one that I know they didn't move. And that was the Ridders cemetery on the east boundary along, I can't remember the name but anyways on the east boundary. Ridders family had their old cemetery there. Quite a few gravestones. And they didn't move that because it was on the boundary. Or close to the boundary. [Ridders family cemetary is on the Corvallis-Independence Road about due east of Coffm Butte, a little north. JRJ
bracketed_corrections: [Ridders family cemetary is on the Corvallis-Independence Road about due east of Coffm Butte, a little north. JRJ...]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there be anybody that you know of that would know where those old pioneer cemeteries have been located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not really. The old timers that know are nearly all gone or moved away.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, your uncle Oswald, he bought the Clarence Wiles place you said.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was in 1942. The same year they bought our place and all the rest of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, where did he live before then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he came out here in '34 from Kansas and I can't remember where exactly all he lived. Until he bought the Clarence Wiles' place. He worked at Wacoma Dairy for a while, I can remember. Maybe that was about all, then he bought Wiles place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he just buy the building or some land there, too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He bought the whole parcel that Clarence Wiles had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, so that didn't get bought up by Adair?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, see this was before Camp Adair. In the '30's, later '30's, when he bought that. And then in '42 when Camp Adair came he had to sell like the rest of us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. So John Wiles only lived there until.. . didn't John Wiles live on the Clarence Wiles place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He lived there as a youth, but when he got married he evidently moved somewhere. I think he was married when Camp Adair came along. Or I think when Oswald bought the place. So he was already probably living in, well I think he worked at Meadowland in Corvallis. So he probably lived in Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So did Clarence Wiles sell the place or did John Wiles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Clarence, yeah, Clarence Wiles sold the place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those are shitepokes. Did you ever hear those called blue herons when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Always shitepokes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Shitepokes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear them called any other names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The landowner could buy the buildings back if he wanted them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so that's how he got the barn and the house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and then we got it through him, you see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When he sold it to Adair, did he continue living around here after?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, north of Albany a ways. Just off the freeway, he bought a farm down in the Deaver area. And he put in a dairy down there for a while. Until the son took it over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How come Clarence Wiles sold that place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he got into the beer distributing business. So he thought, well, farming wasn't profitable enough, so he just as well sell it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so John Wiles got the beer distributing business through his dad?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Through his dad. I'm pretty sure he did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that must have been right after prohibition, then. That they got into beer distributing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I think it was later than that. I think it was a little later than that. Clarence sold milk to Meadowland and somehow or other he got in with Meadowland and Meadowland I think was the one that originally had the beer distributing. I'm not sure, but then later I guess they sold that off. And Clarence probably bought it then. Maybe John bought it, maybe Clarence did something else. Maybe John bought it directly from Meadowland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Did Oswald have any wife and kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, a boy and a girl.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they still alive?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, the one daughter is in California, and the son is in Salem selling recreation vehicles, under the name of Highway Trailer Sales.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so f I want to talk about the Wiles home during the '30's, i'd talk to..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Leighton.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Leighton Rohner?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Leighton Rohner, yes. Down in Salem he goes by the name of George, his middle name, I guess. Or first, I don't know which way. But the business place would be Highway Trailer Sales.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. Black History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, well why don't we start with that then, and Camp Adair, and with the people that were watching you milk.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, they came up, and when the blacks they peered in the window, you know that's what scared the heck out of me. You know we didn't have the barn windows in, it was summer time. The barn windows was out and boy we'd never seen them black ones around, very often, or in Corvallis just one, I think.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, Bud Smith.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Boy, them guys poked their heads in there. Mom and Dad was out hunting farms, I think the whole time. Just Bud and I pretty much at home alone, milking and stuff. And I was about 16, so Bud was about 12 I think. Had to be, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had you ever seen a black guy before?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Just the one in Corvallis [Bud Smith]. And when you see a lot of them it kind of scaxes you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Especially in your own farm, huh?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, really. And then they wanted to watch us milk. And then they got in there and wanted to know how the heck we knew when to quit. We milked by hand, then. And they said, "Well how do you know when to stop? And I said, "Well when the milk quits coming." They was little bit green, they didn't know too much. They seen the pigs out there, the old sow, and she had, I don't know, a whole bunch of little pigs. And they called them, "Oh look at the sheep and all the little lambs!" and it was pig. They was really ignorant them guys, they was from the big city. And then they sucked their eggs. That's what mom got so mad at. They'd

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: come up after that, always to the hen house, and suck our eggs. We had to gather our eggs all during the day every little while, because them blacks like. . . well they worked in grocery stores is what we found out, back east. And they did that in grocery stores, suck the eggs. They taught Bud and I how to suck eggs but I didn't want to suck any. They'd take ahold of both ends and just suck em out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would be the reason they'd do that?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] They liked them. They really liked them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE]ust like stealing watermelons.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, just like stealing watermelons.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a way to get away with taking eggs out of the store.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, they did a lot of crazy things. What else did they. . . oh, the cows chased some of them out. I remember that, Out of the pasture, and they went up over the barb wire fence. Cows scared the holy heck out of them, cause they was all city. Guys from the big city. And the cows looked pretty big.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you family think about them coming around there, did it bother them?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] It didn't seem to bother. We trusted everybody. They went all night, marched up by there the rifle ranges singing them dirty songs. You know, how they sing that when they're marching. We learned quite a few of them goodies. There was a lot of stories about them. I can't really remember too many. I mean I should, I would if could think of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it upset you when Adair first caine in there? Was everybody upset about it being there?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh yeah, they didn't like the idea at first. Well, what upset me was moving from all your friends and stuff. We got strewed everywhere. I mean, some of them went to eastern Oregon, and, oh everywhere. There's quite a few around here. Stockoff, and all that, took off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I haven't heard that name before, Stockoff Who are they?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] They lived in Wells.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] They lived almost in Wells, had a farm there. Yeah, they did own it didn't they? So when Camp Adair came along and bought them out they moved to La Grande.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] La Grande. Henry, and where did the other one go? That lived on

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Carter's place? You know, William was his name wasn't it? Wil Stockoff. I don't remember where they went either, but that was a big worry for me anyway. And then Leighton and then moved clear over to, well it ain't that far but it seemed far then, to Millersburg, out between Albany and Jefferson, sort of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: As long as we're going on Camp Adair, maybe you can go through these Adair photos first. You took them Willie, so.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 2. Powderhouse Photograph

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That's the powderhouse where they stored powder up there, for the blow. You know, like the roads, and on Coffin Butte they blowed rocks, and stuff. They stored all that powder. They had about 4 or 5 of them up in there. And on Beals there was quite a bunch of them. Then they took them out after the soldiers started coming in, they bulldozed that. They went quite a ways back in, if you slipped in when nobody was looking, and looked in, they went in quite a ways in the ground.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you took all these pictures, right?

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 3. Backhoe Photograph

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, I took all them at Camp Adair, yeah. That's the first road that was built in through our place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know the name of that machine there?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh some kind, what do you call them, not a backhoe, not a crane,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, it is a large backhoe.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Is that what it is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, a large backhoe.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, the powderhouse is on your property and...

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And that's on our property. Close to where our house used to be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They'd already taken your house away from there?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] No, our house is still there. Our house should be right up in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this would be to the west of the house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Really, southwest.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, southwest. You can see Beals' hill and our hill, it's right between

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: them. Okay, you say your hill. Did you call it Rohner's hill ever?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] We just called it our hill!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. One of the things I'm trying to do is get names attached to these places. Like, Beals Hill, first time I've heard that name today.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, we always called it Beals Hill. His old turkeys used to come over there, to our place. And dad used to get so mad at them, they'd roost in the trees. And one Thanksgiving clay, that was Ralph and Nell come up from Dffls, my sister and brother-in-law, and we thought, my gosh dad was always bitching about that, we'd go out there and we was gonna get us a turkey. So we went up and it was right in this area here, and we shot one of them things. And old Beal was up on the hill, and his turkeys never come over anymore, after we'd shot it. We'd seen old Gene Beal wandering around. We got that turkey and took off for home, but Ralph and Nell took it home to eat and the darn thing was skinny and tough we couldn't hardly eat it. But his turkeys was over there all the time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, there was lots of grasshoppers. They ate grasshoppers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, Wiese 's, they used to raise turkeys too, and they said in those days they just kept open range on the turkeys.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, well Schulmericks had turkeys that used to come over to our place too.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, I guess they did. But Beals's was always roosting in our trees, and remember, getting in the barn and in the cow mangers? I remember that and dad cussing them out. And, oh, man. That was a mess when you go feed the cows and there'd been some turkeys in there picking out of the mangers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he raise those turkeys for meat or for eggs?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That I don't know. It couldn't have been for meat, they was too dang skinny!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I really don't know.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I couldn't say either, but he had quite a flock of them.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 4. Coffin Butte Blast Photograph

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And that's when they first started taking rock out of Coffin Butte, and they was blowing the rocks to loosen them up. I just happened to get a cloud going up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that's a shot of some of that powder going up?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, powder going up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they're just opening up Coffin Butte as a rock quarry.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 5. Coffin Butte Panorama

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, here's the two [photos] you want made into a panorama.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, yeah. I don't know what to say about that. It's just a picture of Coffin Butte, when they started.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know about how long they'd been working on it at that time?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Really not very long. That went so fast. They had hundreds and hundreds of dynamite boxes up there, and we used to go get them, wood boxes. Really nice boxes, and we'd go get them and pull all the nails out and we used those boxes to move with. In fact, there's still two or three around here, ain't there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah. There were several contractors, it wasn't just one contractor hauling rock. And they each had their own powderhouse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were these local contractors? Did this help local business to put in Camp Adair?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Some of them probably was, but a lot of them was from way out of state.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Some of them was from way out. It was such a large project.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 6. Overpass Photograph

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] See Gene Freeman, remember they used to come up to our place and buy eggs and milk. And I got a picture of him working on this road where you seen that crane, or that backhoe. And he's underneath the cat, with his legs sticking out, but I couldn't find it. I got it at home. And they was from way back somewhere east. And he was working for one of them contractors from back there, that was building that road. Yep, that's the overpass. I don't really know . . . lake, you probably know when that was done, cause you worked on it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, it was done before.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] It was done before we left.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Before we moved over here. And we moved over here in June, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Got over here, it was probably started but we got over here just in time for Bud to go to school in September.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] That late? Oh, I think we bought the place in June and gradually moved over I think in September. Because the renter, that's right, there was a renter on the property and he had to harvest his crops.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I know we moved over here and got over here in time for Bud to go to school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you get hired on to do vely many jobs around Camp Adair there, or was that about.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Just that.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Pause in Recording

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA]. . . in the road, and they all piled in. Whether you had a pickup or car, they didn't ask or nothing. They all piled in and rode to Corvallis with us. I mean, they were all nice guys, really.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: i'm kind of curious about this. Would the black soldiers come into Corvallis at that time?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh yeah, they went. Right along with the whites.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have any trouble with any of the people who were local here or anything?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't really think so. I don't think a bit of trouble. Cause they was soldiers doing their duty and everybody was happy to see somebody in the service. I was, I mean I figured they was doing good. But there was a lot of them blacks, an awful lot of blacks at first. Later on there wasn't so many, but the first group that come there was an awful lot of blacks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the community, there wasn't problems with the people here local?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Not that I know of there. Everybody just accepted them. In fact they gave Bud money when they found that out. . . that was in August, Bud's birthday was August 6, so we were still out there in on August 6, I know we was. But we was talldng when they come to the barn that night. And said it was Bud's birthday. He must have been about 12th birthday or something. And they said good soldiers always give 'em something, and they all give Bud a bunch of money. God, he had a

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: heck of a wad of money before it was over. Like dimes, and quarters, change and stuff. God that was neat we thought. Too bad they weren't there. . . mine was July 1, but they wasn't there yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they came between July and August?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] They must have, or else, that's when they started coming to the barn, anyway, sometime after July 1.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they come eveiy day to watch you milk and stuff, or just every so often?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Every now and then. It seemed like every night there was some around. Be new ones, different ones, just curious about everything. Watch you feed the pigs and all that stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's such a beauqful farm there, they must have been really impressed by it.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well, I suppose. They was impressed by poison oak and all that kind of stuff, too, I know that. They didn't know what that dumb stuff was. In fact they come up to dig some, didn't they. Was it you or dad told them that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I don't remember.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] They was supposed to get some greenery, shrubbery to put around the officers' quarters down there. And the poison oak was real pretty and red. He goes syoU don't want none of that stuff!" They wanted to get a bunch of that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, Ijust found out Beals Hill today, the name that the Anny gave was Poison Oak Hill, that's what's on the maps now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Some of them must have got poison oak.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I heard a lot of them got poison oak. Because they went up through the rifle range and you just waded through poison oak in that. That's all of Camp Adairs buildings, well as they was building them. That was probably about the time we left, that summer. Because it looked like a city down there then, before it was just a house here and there. Stelimachers and Wihiamsons, and a few of them houses. And that's all gone, you can't see any of them now.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 7. Camp Adair Photograph

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, with Bud in the foreground here, this would be somewhere around his birthday, or maybe a little after, in August or September?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Probably in there somewhere. Because it was shortly before we left there. Had to be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wl2at was the reason you decided to take all these pictures?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Because we wasn't supposed to! Somebody, I don't remember whether it was an army officer, or a civilian guy or something. I had the camera once and he says, "No taking pictures because this is government property" you know, and all this kind of stuff. So the more he said that the more I wanted some pictures, because it was wrong I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just cause you were told not to.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, I think that was it. Well, really what I took them for I wanted to remember how it looked. The things going up in there and I thought gosh, I'll forget all of that stuff. Because I remember looking down. . . if you got up on top, if I'd have been way up on top of Coffin Butte then we could have, that would really show them down there. But they're on our hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, here's a...

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 8. Barracks Photograph

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That is a '51 picture when we moved the building up, them was. . . is that what the people stayed in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] The barracks.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] The barracks, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, cause they had showers in there.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And they sold them and we bought one and moved it up on some property. Well you bought, actually bought the property.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said that was Schulinerick's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes. And my father and a neighbor rented it together, and so when the property was sold after it ended, Camp Adair, the owner of the property had first choice to buy it back. And if not, then the renter had next choice. So as a renter I bought the property back for my brother. And I think that's about the time he was in the Sea Bees, wasn't he?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well, yeah, just about the time he went in. '50 1 think you bought, and

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: we bought the buildings right, almost right then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's a picture of the building being put on the Schulmerick place then?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] After it was up there on the side of the hill a little ways, there was a little flat spot. Now it's christmas trees where the building was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody ever use that building?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It was never used.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] We ate lunch in it when we used to farm out there, that was about it. Oh, and that was before Camp Adair even thought about coming in. I don't know what this is, don't have no date on it, does it [referring to photograph].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was the last of the Adair pictures. This is pictures of the Rohner farm and family, now.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 9. Rohner Family Photograph

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were the one that knew the names of the people in that, Willie, so that's why I'm handing them to you.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Okay, well. From the left to the right here, the front row then. That's my brother Bud, or Ed I guess we're supposed to call him. We always called him Bud. And that's my sister Elsie. And that's myself. And then over here on the left to the right again, that's lake, and my brother-in-law Ralph. And my sister Nell, or Neffie. My brother-in-law Merle Prindle. His wife was my sister Sam, she won't let me use her full name, well she's Selma. But she hates it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Her full name is Selma. She was named after Mrs. Glender, because Mrs. Glender helped when she was born. So that's where she got the name Selma.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You told me that story before and we didn't record it. Can you tell me how Mrs. Glender helped in the birth of.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well I don't know actually for sure whether she helped in the birth or helped take care of her afterwards.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't know that either, but I know later when I was born Dr. who come out? I heard Mom say some doctor come out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] We were all born on the farm.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Was it Dr. Ball?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] There was a Dr. Ball, but I don't know if it was him.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't know either.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] More likely it was Johnson.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yes, I've heard of Johnson. Dr. Tartar [a fine doctor and person] came out when you got your fingers cut off. Or was it Johnson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] He was the Doctor, Johnson, that did it, but Dr. Tartar was in medical school and he came out with Dr. Johnson; he was home and he came out with Dr. Johnson.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 10. Baldy and Prince Photograph

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That's mom and dad there on the right. That's dad, and then Baldy and Prince. What he did, he had a sled. He used that sled to haul corn or potatoes, or junk up from the field. An old home made sled. It did have steel runners on it I think.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, nairow wagon tire steel runners on it. Liners.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said "Baldy" but Jake, you said 'Rally."

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, dad always said "Bally" but it was supposed to be "Baldy".

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] But mom and dad was Swiss and when they talked they didn't talk real plain.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] They pronounced a little different.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] They pronounced a lot of things different. Prunes were Prunz, remember?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you grow up speaking the Swiss language too?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, I could. . .never did talk it much but I can understand it, yeah. The way mom talked anyway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recognize the details along the hill there? There's a strange design in there?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
