entries.text: [WILMA] Well, that's a fence. Up there, the fence row. Separating our place and the Butte.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, that draw there it looks like there's some odd vegetation. It almost looks like something's planted above it.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That I wouldn't know. Far as I ever knew there was just pasture grass

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: and it was different on the other side of the Butte, was all barley beard.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I think that was, there was grass on the hill and some of that area was a little more rocky and the grass didn't grow on it. I think is what that is.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Didn't you at one time plant Sudan grass up there? I thought you did.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No Sudan grass there.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Where did you plant some Sudan grass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Sudan grass wouldn't grow up there. It's a different kind.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I thought one time you guys planted something up there. But the Coffin Butte was all barley beard.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] That's like a foxtail grass.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Got between your toes, and the dogs' toes used to fester up. And the socks. Gosh, it got into everything.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 11. Coffin Butte Fires

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that a native grass?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That's native, and it grew. . . and I remember Leighton and Bud set it on fire one time when it was dry. Do you remember that? You guys had to fight it. Man, that field burned twice that I seen. Just the grass, it didn't get into the trees. Man, when that's lit it just zipped up there through that dry foxtail. I mean it just went 90 miles an hour, didn't it. Just poof and it's gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm really interested in that. How did the fires get started?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well, Bud and Leighton was wanting to see if it'd burn! And they had been smoking a little, they was just little. Gosh, Bud must have been about 7 or 8 years old. Real young. And they was, Bud was walking, going home with Leighton. And they decided to stop and have a cigarette and then they decided to see if that grass would burn, and WOOF. And they all run to somewhere and hid and Les Davis and Uncle Oswald and all them come to fight fire. It burned quite an area that time. But one time the whole thing burned, I don't know how that started.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I think . . . it seems like it burned off three or four times altogether.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well, I can remember twice.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was still burning even in fairly recent times. Do you remember it burning after World

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: War 11?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No, I don't.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] No, because we didn't live out there. It might have, all right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, it's possible.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Because before it did, I know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How fast did it burn?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, I don't know, but it burns fast. It just seems like you light it and it's all.. . well, it's just dry and dead. And once it gets about that high it just waves in the wind.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Generally gets lit down at the bottom and its uphill and naturally burns faster uphill than it would downhill or on a level.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But not hot enough to catch the trees on fire?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, it didn't get up into the trees.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] No, well there wasn't so much barley beard right up on top that'd got in. And they could stop it up there with gunny sacks. That's all they ever fought it with was gunny sacks and water buckets. And that's all anybody had. They didn't have any fire equipment. They'd sure beat them in, I know you swing them sacks.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Five gallon bucket with water in it. And put your gunny sacks in and soak them and start swatting, and then soak it again and swat some more.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] But we used to ride down. . . the tobaggon or sled would go as fast or faster on that stuff than it did the snow. Ask Babe Studack, he got his mouth full of barley beards and it darned near killed him. He had his mouth open. They're kind of like. . . well when they get in you know they don't want to, they want to go on through, you can't pull them back out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Do you know what foxtail grass is?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, but I think I know what barley beard is.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It's got a point where the seed is and then the beards go out like this all the way around. And the whole thing is probably not wider than my little fingernail. With a point. It only goes one way, it gets in your clothes it only goes one way in. But you can't back it out. You've got to pull it clear through. Gets up your nose there's no way you can get it out of your nose, hardly, other than fishing it out with

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: something.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, and we used to pull it out of the dogs' feet. Dogs' feet used to get it terrible. Their feet would swell up like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you'd ride the toboggans down?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, we used to, Bud and I did with Leighton and Babe Studack and other kids. Boy you'd just go like a.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you do it all the time or just every so often?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, now and then but we had to learn to keep our mouth shut, because when them things flew in you couldn't get them out, hardly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: After the fires burned, do you remember how the grasses came in after that?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well as soon as it rained I imagine it just turned green again. The hill was just beautiful in the spring. When the barley beards was green and starting to grow, but as summer come they died, made seeds and died.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It's an annual grass. So then there's seed in the ground from before that didn't sprout, and well even some of the burnt seed that didn't get too hot. Seed part would drop down and the first rains would sprout it and it would become green again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any taiweed or anything up on there?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Later years not so much, but I can remember earlier years, especially Baldy, with that white face, and cows and everything would come in there, the whole face, lower part of their face would be all tarry, sticky, and nasty.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Sticky, geez.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] All this gooey stuff. But I don't know what happened to the tarweed. Whether it got a disease or something. But it was awful bad. Way back. But as the years. . . by the time we left Camp Adair, I don't think we ever saw it anymore.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Not much anymore. Oh, I remember our pant legs just get covered with them seeds.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It was a problem with grass hay, too. A lot of tarweed in the grass hay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it just kind of disappeared over time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah. Whether it got a disease or what I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about in the flats. Did you ever notice, say around the water or any of the flats,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Canuzs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, when we lived out at Camp Adair I didn't know what it was. But since we moved over here, in the river bottom there's some back water down in there and a friend told us that that was Camas and that the Indians used to use Camas for food.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you recognized it from earlier. Was it a familiar plant, like one that you can remember from the family farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] We didn't have any on our farm, no camas.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] All we had was rose bushes. Lot of little rose bushes. They used to eat them rose hips, the Indians did. I always heard, wild roses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about wild onions?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh yeah, we had quite a few wild onions in one field, next to Beals. There in that southwest corner. Yes. And you could sure tell it in the milk, we didn't dare turn the milk cows in that field because they'd eat the garlic and you could taste the garlic in the milk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any of the wildflowers up on Coffin Butte, Willie?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh I remember I went up years and years ago when Studacks come out, every Easter, man the dogwood and the ladyslippers. We went down there and picked them ladyslippers all the time. They just grew in one area, where there was a few fir. There just wasn't many fir trees on Coffin Butte. And they grew under the fir trees. And that was our big thing Easter Sunday was to have an easter egg hunt. Mom had the Studacks for dinner. Well, see they didn't have a car, we had to bring them out and take them back. That seemed like a long ways to Corvallis in them days. And Mom would have a big dinner and we'd have an easter egg hunt and then head up the hill. Ladyslippers and johnny jump-ups, and lamb tongues, and then bird bills, and then cat ears. Remember the cat ears?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, they were a little later, usually.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, they was later. There was several kinds. And violets, we used to call them violets.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Johnny jump-ups?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] No, they was little blue. They had just little dinky blue flowers on there. Not violets. Spring beauties, we called them spring beauties.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The ladyslippers, were they the little pink ladyslippers?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, just little dinky, dainty. They didn't have a stem over that long.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, yeah, it was longer. It was about like this.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Was it? Well they seemed shorter to me. Well, probably the way we picked them for Mom, a bouquet, we probably just had heads, I don't know. I know it was always kind of spooky down in that fir timber when I was little. Later I got to like it, but when I was smaller I thought, boy it's dark.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Bears.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, we heard bear stories, and then there was supposed to be Indian graves up there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 12. Indian Graves

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you heard stories about Indian graves up on Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, we did. I always heard they was dug out over towards Kester's end, the east end. [Wes Kester was renting the Walter Wiles farm when Camp Adair came in. JR]
bracketed_corrections: [Wes Kester was renting the Walter Wiles farm when Camp Adair came in. JR]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Over on Walter Wiles' end of butte.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] There was, you could see. I mean, it looked just like a grave. We'd go up there when we was kids and look around. They said the big guys, kids that was bigger than us, supposedly had dug some up. I don't know, that's the stories we always heard that the ones that was just a little older than us dug them out. We'd stand there and wonder if they missed anything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And the later ones that came probably said the older ones like us.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Like us dug them out, I suppose. But there was, I mean you could see they was just about the size of a grave, the little holes. Where they didn't fill them in right. Used to was that way years and years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was stories of Indian graves and you actually went to spots where you thought the Indians had been buried.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah. That was right square on top of the hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, right on the top.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the very peak.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, just as you go into the timber, the wooded area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] On the east end.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] So we heard all kinds of stories. And I think there was because we used to go over there and look and then we'd always think what're we gonna do if we see a skull. Wes Kester had a skull but I don't know where in the Sam heck he got it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, they dug it up down at Vanderpools, do you remember they took out, the Army engineers took out a lot of gravel down at Vanderpools. Oh, Guy Dairy did it, too, and that's where they found this Indian skull.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well I know he had that dumb skull and it was kind of spooky. When you're young.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I don't know how he got a hold of it, but somebody must have gave it to him.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Somebody must have. I always wondered, I used to want to think it come from Coffin Butte, so I figured there was some rolling around up there. But now at Merle's place, ain't that the old, some old trail on top of Merle's field?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, there was a trail over the top of that. That was down in the Suver area, west of Suver. There was a trail.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I forgot what they called it. That old road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That'd be Merle. . .?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Prindle, my brother-in-law.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he's got an old trail through his property?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Up on top of the hill, it was. Or they always said it was, where the old some kind of trail went. I wished they'd have stopped here, the turkeys.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's one thing I'm real interested in, is Indian graves and wildflowers and these old trails, how they all interact. After Coffin Butte had burned, would you notice there would be more or less wildflowers, or more or less or a certain kind of grass?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] On the south side where the burn was there was never no flowers, other than buttercups, or something like that growing there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] There was, down over Wiles side, there used to be yellow snapdragons that grew in, there was little gullies coming down. Where water would seep out later in the spring.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] But on the face of the south side of the hill it just was nothing really but foxtail grass. Till you get to the top. Right up as soon as you got where the timber started, it would be jolly jumpups and bird bills, was always right up on top, right where the timber started. [Bird bills came a little after lamb's tongues, about the same time as ladyslippers. Cat ears grew along the Butte base. Excavations took them all out. Cartwheels: 4-6 inches, flat like a spoked wheel, reddish-pink with white border. And there are no more jackrabbits. WR]
bracketed_corrections: [Bird bills came a little after lamb's tongues, about the same time as ladyslippers. Cat ears grew along the Butte base. Excavations took them all out. Cartwheels: 4-6 inches, flat like a spoked wheel, reddish-pink with white border. And there are no more jackrabbits. WR]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And the ladyslippers and dogwood were a little bit over the hill. And the lambs tongues. They was always just before you went down over into the timber.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 13. Jackrabbits

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about grosses. Were there bunch grosses, other types of grasses that you can remember? Native grasses?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I didn't pay too much attention to grasses in those days. Lot of graydiggers, I know that was our biggest sport. Dad bought me a .22 and a whole carton of shells, he'd hide them things, the shells in his sock drawer. I knew where they was at. And he'd just dole them out. Cause they was kind of spendy, you know in them days they didn't have much money. And he'd dole us out a box and it was supposed to last us all week and it'd last a day or something. And we'd have to go steal one. And I know he must have missed them. And then I didn't think he'd know the difference. And there, every little bit of graydigger holes there on the side, wasn't there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, there'd be regular trails through the foxtails, down to our fields, see. And there'd be a hole off to the side, and then another little hole off to the side. And another one. And they'd all come down that same runway, and then there'd be other runways through there. And they'd fill those old pockets full of grain, you know, and then go on up and store it, see, and back down again, for another round.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] When they thought they'd seen somebody they'd set there by the hole, and look around, had their feet down like that. And we'd shoot them. That was more fun! And jackrabbits was thick in them days out there, on Schulmerick's place. We used to go over there and shoot jackrabbits in the evening. At night. I mean them

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: was genuine jackrabbits, they wasn't just cottontails. And then they all disappeared after a while.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, they got a disease, and I don't know but what maybe somebody introduced that disease to get rid of them.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] You never see a jackrabbit. . . I seen one or two in all the years since.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when the jackrabbits died out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, gee...

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That was just shortly before we come over here they started thinning out. Probably finished 'em in World War II.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Probably '35 to '40 was when they.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Was dwindling down, but there was still a bunch out there when we left, was some, but I imagine the soldiers pot shotted at them. I wouldn't doubt it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That snow in 1937. Do you remember anything about that?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Our barn fell down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Your barn fell down?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, the roof caved in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Fell down. And one-fourth of it, or half of one side, the lower half, that's where we kept the cows, and they were facing toward the middle, and there was so much weight on it that it just bucked the wall on the outside, and so the outside, it come down, and so did the hay mow. There was no more support for the hay mow so it came down. But the front side, just above the stanchion stayed, and it hit the cows' tail bone.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] The ones that was laying down wasn't hurt.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It didn't hurt them. But the ones that were standing, it skinned up their tail bones. I didn't see all that because I was in California at that time.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] The snow was three foot deep or better.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And so they wrote me letter to come on home, the barn fell down. And I never did get that letter.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] You never got it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No, I never got. And then they wrote again, and found out about that time a plane went down with a bunch a mail near San Francisco, somewhere down in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So evidently the letter was on that, so I didn't get home for, I don't know, 2 months or more, after the barn fell down.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't remember. . . all I remember is we milked outside. We milked outside.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could that snow have anything to do with those jackrabbit populations going down?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] It didn't really last that long, that snow, I don't remember how long that lasted. But it usually melted soon.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It was a disease, really. Because they got, down around their belly they got these.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Warbles, or something, didn't they.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Almost like your fist, abscesses.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] We called them warbles.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] There used to be a lot of jackrabbits. I remember one time my father and I went in the Model T and Albert Zundt was with us. We went up Sulphur Springs Road, I don't remember who we went to see, whether it was the Goviers or what, but we were going up that way, and a rabbit run across the road. And we heard it hit, so we stopped and got out of the Model T, and went back to hunt for the rabbit. And we couldn't find it no rabbit anywhere. And we walked around in front of the car and there was the rabbit hanging on the crank handle, it had pierced his body and there he was hanging on the crank handle.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was a whole bunch ofjackrabbits and then now there's none. And they all pretty much died out in that five year period?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Somewhere, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow. Was there any coyotes or anything feeding that were feeding on them? Or any raptors?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Mom used to talk about coyotes howling years ago.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, that's when we lived on the Writsman place.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Steel Hill, what she called Steel Hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, that's right. Mom always called that the Steel Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What we're calling Writsman 's Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah. I'd forgotten all about that. That's right.

chapters.title: Chicken Hawks, Bears, and Bee Trees

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Remember I was asking you about the Steels and you said you'd heard something about them but you couldn't remember what.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] But Mom used to tell me that they, when they lived up there on that place that she used to hear the coyotes up on the Steel Hill. But I never did see one, I never seen a fox out there, and you seen a deer about once or twice a year that would come through there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] We see more deer here than there.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, a heck of a lot more deer here. Well, now they're thick through Camp Adair, and have been, well, ever since Camp Adair. We started hunting then. But before, it was just -- I mean when somebody seen a deer, like in the 1930's, everybody hollered and called the others, "Look, look there's a deer!" I mean, it was really something to see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear of any elk in thai area at all?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Never then. But there has been up on Merle's place since Camp Adair.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 14. Chicken Hawks, Bears, and Bee Trees

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any eagles or hawks, or owls?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Hawks, there was a lot of hawks.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] We used to shoot them all the time, we called them chicken hawks. They'd catch the chickens.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well they did pack our chickens off. The young ones.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And the chickens, boy they'd see a hawk and they'd really run for the chicken house to hide. So we always called them chicken hawks. And we'd shoot them every time we got a chance.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Dang right. Up on the Butte and around they'd pick them up and they'd go up there and eat them, and you could see piles of feathers where they'd pack the chickens off and eat the chickens. Of course rabbits they did the same way.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] See in those days every farmer had chickens. But now there's just chicken ranches once in a while, so they don't cause no problems for them. And I wouldn't shoot a hawk anymore on a bet. I cleared some land down there in the river bottom

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: one year, and noticed there was a hawk nest in one big cottonwood tree, and we worked down there for a month or more clearing the land, and we left that tree because of this hawk nest. We could see the hawks sitting up on the edge of the nest flapping their wings like this, practicing you see. So we got all done except that one tree, and we figured well those hawks could fly by now, so if we pull that tree over they'll fly out of the nest. So we rocked that tree back and forth and they just hung on the nest like this, you know. And finally the tree got loose and it come on over and they just hung on the nest until it hit the ground and the cottonwood limbs just disintegrated and they killed them you see. Well we found 11 or 12 gopher skulls in that nest. And I didn't realize they caught gophers. And so I wouldn't shoot one on a bet now. And there is no reason to shoot one now, nobody has chickens except the chicken ranchers. [MRS. J. ROHNER] I would have if my husband would let me. [JAKET They'd all get killed here on the highway, so.. [MRS. I. ROHNER] Not if they were fenced in.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I remember though, lake, that one time there was a bald eagle out there. Around Coffm Butte. I remember that, and dad had us look because it was an eagle. Maybe you was gone then, too. He was kind of a dang bum, he took off.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I used to shoot at 'em, I was kind of a poor shot!

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Boy, I loved pheasants, that was the best meat there was to eat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about bob whites, do you remember bob whites?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah. We had meadowlarks out there too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened to them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I don't know, they just gradually disappeared.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And we had pigeons, wild pigeons out there, big herds on our field all the time. Herds of wild pigeons. I used to go up and shoot them, all the time. And what else did we have. The only bear I ever seen, but that was after we'd come over here, was when Bud was in the service. I went back out there hunting deer, I mean the deer started coming in down at Camp Adair, I seen that darn bear and I wouldn't

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: tell anybody because I knew they wouldn't believe me. And then Ray Novak seen him too, so then I could tell my bear story. I thought it was a black angus calf there on our place, until it jumped over this. . . I seen this black and this critter that looked like a black angus. And I thought, God, I wonder whose got cattle up here? And then I went along a little further and the dumb thing took over a log, and then I realized it weren't a black angus and I got kind of chicken and I didn't hunt much longer. Come home and just kept my mouth shut until Ray Novak at church that night said that there had been a bear out there then I got to talk about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever see any bobcats, or cougars?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Not out there, not that I remember. But I heard stories about cougars, like I say further back than the Steel lull and stuff. They said, because I used to hear them tell how what an awful sound they make, if you heard one they'd make your hair stand up and I remember the people talking about it, but that was back the other way, west of us.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't know, about, just two or three years before we moved over. That's them flying squirrels. They glide, you know. We'd try to catch them all the time, and we caught one that bit me in the ankle. I stepped on him, part of him, his tail, and he whipped around. We was gonna pick him up, but found out we couldn't do that. The kids, the guys, well Ernie Kester I think and Bud, I don't remember who, they'd climb up a tree to get them to come down. They don't really fly, you know, they just glide down. So we'd run after them, we was supposed to catch one of them. But there was one tree there on the side there of Schulmericks Hill, an old dead maple that had them in it. So we did a lot of flying squirrel chasing. Only ones I ever seen out there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When was that, about the 1930's?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, probably. Or might be '40. Just before Camp Adair come in a while. Yeah, it was probably around '39 or '40. Remember the flying squirrels and Schulmericks? Ernie Kester, and Bud and I and Patsy and a bunch of those kids, you know.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It was before the '40's.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Let's see, Bud wasn't. . . it had to be not too much before the '40's, because Bud went to the 8th grade over here in Oakville in '42. And he was big enough to climb way the heck and gone up in them trees, him and Ernie Kester to chase them out. And that tree was just full of woodpecker holes. I mean just literally covered. An old maple tree down that gully at Schulmericks. That's where we always chased them out and tried to catch them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] There was a lot of bee trees around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bee trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Bee trees. Wild bees.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh yeah. Swarms come through there all the time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Coffm Butte. We dropped several of them at Coffin Butte. I'd sneak up into Schulmericks and Beals when I shouldn't have. Drop some bee trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the bee trees in old dead trees? Were there a lot of snags?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No, they'd be mostly trees that the center would be rotted out, the heart part, and maybe a limb and then there'd be a knot hole or something. Or a crack, a flaw in the tree and crack, and they would come in and build inside the tree. I have seen them in fir trees, most generally they were in maple trees, older trees where the centers were rotted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it'd be a live tree with a dead center but it'd usually be a hardwood, like oak or maple?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah. Usually.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 15. Father and Calves Photograph

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Here's a picture of your dad there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes. This was a long long time ago. With the brown swiss calves.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Is that Dad?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Urn hmm.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That's pretty old.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's that building on the right there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] The chicken house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And did you build that?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Shorty did.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, we had a Swiss man there. He was a planer man by trade, and he run planers. And at that time he was running the planer down at Wells Dale for, I think didn't they call it Valley Lumber? [Lumber was shipped from the mill near the Soap Creek Schoolhouse in 1928 by Model T trucks. After running through the planing mill in Wells, it was shipped by rail. JR]
bracketed_corrections: [Lumber was shipped from the mill near the Soap Creek Schoolhouse in 1928 by Model T trucks. After running through the planing mill in Wells, it was shipped by rail. JR]

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Valley Lumber, I think it was Bill..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Bill Bertram and McCoy, can't remember his first name, were partners in the mill. And they hired him to run the planer.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And he boarded with us, Mom fed him, bedded him, washed his clothes, made his lunch, he boarded there at our house, that way she made some extra money.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] That was my mother's money, boarding him and the chickens, whatever the chickens brought in, that was her money.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that's why she had him build the chicken house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, I guess he had time in between.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, they didn't work Saturdays and Sundays, and they got off early, I mean worked 8 hours, where farmers work a lot longer. And then he'd work at that whenever he felt like it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] We put in over 12 hours a day on the farm, because we'd get up in the morning to milk the cows and then we'd eat breakfast quick, go out in the field again and come in at noon, to eat, back to the field, then come in again for supper. We usually ate supper before milking.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] It depended. In the wintertime sometimes after milking, but in the summer before. And during combine, not combine, but thrashing time, Mom and the kids had to milk. The little kids. You guys used to didn't milk then because they worked til what 7 or 8 o'clock with the thrashing machine.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 16. Rohner Farm Photograph

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] So it was long hours on the farm. Here's a picture of our place from near the top of Coffin Butte, looking at our place and Beals Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you tell me the. . . there is an oak tree in the middle.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] The story there, yes. There was a story that a man lived there in a little

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: brick building or house, just a very small, just a man alone. And that he had buried some gold around near that tree, and we never did, of course we didn't have metal detectors then, we never did find any. But finally we later cleared that land except for that oak tree, and farmed it, and we would find the remnants of bricks, particles of bricks in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you actually were able to find the bricks.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear the name of the man that lived there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I probably did but I can't remember if I did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It wasn't Hodge, Hodges?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I have no idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or Cahoon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] If I at one time knew the name, it's gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you hear how he got his gold?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No. No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Willie, did you ever hear any stories about buried gold other than this gold in that neighborhood?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well there was tales of people burying out there but I don't really definitely remember any certain stories other than that one that was supposed to be on our place. But I've heard other stories around, you have too, I'm sure, didn't you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well if I did I've forgotten them.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't really know where at, but I've heard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear any stories about Tampico?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't know too much about Tampico.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I just heard that it was a wild place, they had this saloon, and stage coaches stopped there, and that's about it.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Mostly, it seems like our end was pretty much Wellsdale.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] We didn't visit too much back there, only when we walked across the pasture to get there because it was five miles around the road either way to go visit people in the Tainpico area through there.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] We used to play ball, our little old Welisdale School, we did have ball

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: teams that played Tampico and Soap Creek and Suver.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] That was after my time.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That was after your time, that was in the late '30's and '40's, when I was going to school. Boy we thought that was the greatest, man, we'd go play ball. One time one year we got to ride on the.. . instead of riding our bicycles we got to ride on the, what do you call them Jake? Scooters, that went down the railroad track and took the men down the track?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, the section crew you know, had those things they'd pump em by hand.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, but this one was motorized.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, that was motorized.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] At the time that we come. And they took us, we was gonna ride our bicycles down, and they said they was going to Suver and that we could ride down on their Scoot whatever it was, and some of us rode down on it. Boy that was a thrill. We had cheap thrills back in them days, compared to now!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tobogganing on grass?

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 17. Gold Oak Tree Photograph

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah. That's just the picture of that gold tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, it's got some stock in there too.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And the straw stack there and all our brown swiss. I just was always kind of proud of them dumb old cows. I loved them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many did you have, about?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] We probably, we milked about 20 out there didn't we? One time we had more than the stanchions would hold at one time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes. Well didn't we bring about 20 cows over here?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I think so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And I remember we sold several at the auction.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] But see, in them days, there was just lake, if you could get him out of bed, and boy dad had an awful time with that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Dad would turn on the radio real loud.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Real loud. Montana Slim.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Montana Slim. And that woke me up.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That meant milking time. There was just three of us that milked. You and I and dad, wasn't it? And we had to milk them this way so you didn't get to milk 50 60 cows, man you'd peter out before too long, but 20 some was an awful lot to milk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any other families thai had brown swiss?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well, Uncle Oswald had some, but not as many, a few. There wasn't too many brown Swiss around here. We always had to go quite a ways to get our bulls, didn't we, new bulls. In fact, you guys went down to Ashland or somewhere one year.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] One year we went down to Ashland and stayed with some friends that used to live in Corvallis, over night, and then got up to go back. Another time we went up to Washington, close to the Seattle area.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, and then we got quite a few there from Meyer, or something, wasn't that, around Beaverton or Portland area, up in there, but there was very few Brown Swiss around here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason you had them?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Because, I guess because they was home to mom and dad. I mean that's what they had over in Switzerland. They're nice and fat, Dad always said they was easy keepers, they foraged a lot. They could get their own feed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] They're a sturdy animal. And good milkers, not as much milk as a Holstein, but richer.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Not as much rich as a Jersey. But if they wasn't any good for milk, you had some meat. Where on a Jersey you didn't have no meat.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, an animal if something went wrong with it, like maybe, three fits went bad or something, or it didn't produce very well, you had a lot of beef there to sell. Where with a Jersey you didn't. And weight wise they even beat the Holstein some.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And they always looked nice and fat, where a Holstein when they milk heavy, they look kind of lean and lanky.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 18. Stellmacher House Photograph

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who's that, can you tell?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That is a picture, I know two of my sisters was there, but I don't know who the third person is, and I can't see it good enough. But that's just the old home, just the way it looked when we was gonna have to leave before too long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't think we've put anything on the tape about where that house came from.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, that house came from the Steilmacher place, about a mile and a half to the east. And Steilmachers built a new house, and then the person that bought this place, from Joe Smith, decided to buy that house and move it. So they put four wagons under it, one under each corner, and they moved it up there, cut some trees and stuff to get through, and moved it clear to the back end of the farm. Why they chose the back end of the farm, I don't know, because there was that much more road to build and that much farther to move the house. So then the fellow gave up the place, decided he couldn't make the payments or something, I don't know, so Joe Smith repossessed it, then he sold it to my father and mother. And it was still on skids, the house when they bought it. So they put it down on the foundation, and my father built a road into it, it was all rock out of the rock quarry that we started on Coffin Butte on the east end of our place, and rocked the road.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Do you suppose that's the only place maybe they could get good water or something? Who dug that well? Did dad do it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Dad dug the well. So it wasn't because of the well.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That was good water.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It seemed so ridiculous to put the house on the far side of the place when they had to build the road because they could have got by with half as much road as we put on there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it more private there maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, there wasn't no problem with privacy, then, because there weren't that many close neighbors.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] About one car every five or ten minutes went by on the highway down there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] The ground sloped a little bit where the house was, not all that much. But

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: it, on the north end of the house, was practically on the ground and the south end was up off the ground a foot or so or a little over. And we, when we were kids we were shy, and we'd see a car coming up the road visiting. We'd, the three of us. . . I was probably instigator.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Probably, I don't remember that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] There was just three of us then, so we'd run under the house and hide when a car would come up the road.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 19. Rohner Family

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've got three other photos here. Now these are dferent because they are not on the family home and they don't have anything to do with Camp Adair.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, this was Uncle Oswald, and myself and a cousin, Lucille Kobler.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's up at the Wiles place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] That's up at Clarence Wiles house, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. When did he purchase that house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I really can't remember just when he purchased that house. Did he first rent the place and then buy it, or did he...

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] He must have. I can't remember.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Or did he buy it and move on it? I have no idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why did he move out here from Kansas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] During a drought. 1930 drought. They'd had several years. Fact is, I was back there in 1934, and he had just wrote to my father how things were in Oregon and if there was a chance to come out. And so, when I came there I talked to him some so he decided to move out. And so he sold his cattle, the government paid him according to quality and size I believe it was 8 to 12 dollars a head, or 12-1/2 a head for the cattle, and then they slaughtered the cattle and then they used it for relief families.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well then his sister and brother-in-law, Aunt Agnes, they come out at the same time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, they came out too. And they had several years of drought. And I know, I helped a cousin back there, Clifford Higer, for about a month while I was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: there and we dug a well to water the garden and stacked Russian thistles for hay. And that's all they had for feed. And that Russian thistle grows kind of like a big ball, when its, the branches come up and off the main root and go out in kind of a ball, and sometimes it can grow several feet high. And a lot of times a lot shorter. So they'd hoe it off and then break 'em, and all you've got is a lot of fluff. And then stack them. And my job was up on the stack to lay them all Out and stomp them down, and you was wading up to your neck in those Russian thistles, but you would stomp and weight it down. I was still pulling stickers out after we got to Oregon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So then your Aunt came ow at the same time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, my Aunt, and then my Uncle, and then my uncle's brother-in-law, and mother. So there was three families that came out at the same time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And did they settle in the Coffin Butte area too, or just off.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Leslie Davis and his mom lived in Studack's place a very short time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] That's right, they did.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Grandma Davis and Les. For a while, yeah. And Uncle Oswald was on Wiles's place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] First, he worked for Wacoma Dairy for a while.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah. And Uncle John and Aunt Agnes Weder went down to Williamsons and worked on that dairy.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Cleve Williamson, which was across the road from Steilmachers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So at one time you had Rohners in three farms right around the Coffin Butte there.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, well one of them was Rohner, the other was Weder, but it was a Rohner, the woman was a Rohner. And the Davis, that was in-laws.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did the Davis's live?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] On Studack's place, they moved in where Studack lived for a while. Him and his. . . it was a man and his mother. He was single. He never got married until, oh, a long time later. He was older when he got married.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 20. Studack and Zundt Accident

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: While we're on Studack, why don't we skip back to there. That's that part that 1 fouled up before. Can you tell the stoly about how the Studacks purchased that property and what they

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: did for a living?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, well, they purchased the property from Mr. Wiles, Ed Wiles, and I don't remember how big, but I would say at least 60 acres, possibly a little more. And they built a house on it, and a barn. And then to supplement his income he worked for Alvie Govier. Well, I don't know whether he ever worked right in the sawmill, but he felled timber for him, I know, later at least. And then Albert Zundt, who was a friend of the Studacks, and maybe he was even, was he related to them, or not?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't really think so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Just a friend from Switzerland. He came several years later.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How was Studack related?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] My mother's first cousin. So Albert came a little later over here, and then they went, well Albert worked a little bit too, didn't he?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That I don't know. I was pretty small.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, anyway along the line he went to work for Alvie Govier too, so the two of them felled timber for Alvie Govier, and he in 1928, early in 1928, he studied for his citizenship. For one reason he wanted to be a citizen, and another reason he wanted to vote that fall because he believed in Alfred E. Smith. So he got his citizenship papers, a little later in the summer, and so he decided to vote for Alfred E. Smith. So they were about to have a baby and, would you say four weeks?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And so, in probably close to October, anyway, Mrs. Studack was about to have a baby, and so Mr. Studack was killed in the woods. Oh yeah, they had decided to name the baby Alfred, after Alfred E. Smith. And so anyway, Albert Zundt and Mr. Studack were working in the woods at Goviers, falling timber, and a limb caine down and hit him on the head. Wounded him terribly. And they took him to the hospital, and in 24 hours or something he died. And Alfred was born about 4 weeks before Mr. Studack was killed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But he didn't have a chance to vote then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No, he didn't get a chance to vote because he was killed before the election.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is Alfred Studack still alive?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, he lives in Salem, he works in a bank, he's been a banker all his life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then the family, after he was killed, they had to move, didn't they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Didn't Rosie stay there a while, didn't Albert stay with her some?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I believe maybe that's right. I think Albert took care of things for a while there, a year or two maybe.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And then she moved to town.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And then she decided to move to town, but then Albert Zundt bought the place. And he farmed a little and he raised mink.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Mink, yeah. Used to go fishing where the sewer run into Corvallis, or something, down by the river.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And he asked me to go along several different times, to help him fish,

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Catch suckers, you know, and all that yucky stuff.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Where these, I think they had three big sewer lines from Corvallis that dumped directly into the river, raw sewage. And we'd fish in that area and catch these suckers and stuff like that for mink feed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Studack farm became a mink farm, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many mink did he raise at one time?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I have no idea.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] He had quite a lot of them but I have no idea how many, whether it was 50 or 200, I don't know. I don't think maybe he had all that many, but he had quite a few.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] And he logged, too, or kept logging.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes, he kept logging, and he horse logged. He had a team of big horses, and horse logged. So he horse logged, this was in 1928 when Studack got killed, and he logged until about 1935 was it?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Somewhere in there. I was still fairly young when he got killed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, it must have been '35, because he was killed after I got back from my trip in '34, so about '35 and possibly '36.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Right in there somewhere when he got killed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] When he got killed, he was putting logs on the rollaway and doing something and a log rolled over him and he was crushed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he'd stayed living at that same place until that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Miat happened after he got killed? He was a bachelor?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened to the place after he got killed?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] George Adams probably the next one that lived there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I think so. George Adams owned it, and I presume, as I remember it, I think he bought it from the estate. And what money that he had went probably to Switzerland because he had no relatives in this country.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: George Adams was Swiss?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No, I mean Albert Zundt. The money that George Adams paid to the estate you see probably then went to Switzerland because there was no relatives over here.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well Albert was the one that took all his dishes to the creek and washed them. His skillets and stuff in the gravel, wasn't it. He scoured his skillets in the grave.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I remember Wes Kester, he always admired him. He could out. . . Albert was quite husky and Wes Kester was very very strong for his size, but he wasn't all that big. So Albert could outlift him. For one thing they'd get on a set of platform scales, sit on it and then reach underneath and pull to see how many hundred pounds they could pull down besides their own weight on the scales. Albert Zundt could beat him at that. And something or other, oh, arm twisting and one thing and another. Because he was real powerful. Oh Wes, he went up to visit Albert one Sunday and so Albert had a fish fry, fish I suppose he caught in Soap Creek. There used to be trout in Soap Creek. So I remember Wes Kester telling about Albert after they had the fish fry, Albert went to the creek, the little gravel bar out in the creek, and put a little soap in there and scooped up some gravel and kept swinging it around and had the old pan real shiny.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was pretty impressed by that. What happened to his mink after he got killed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] He might have parted with those just before.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I think he did. I don't think he haLl mink anymore when he got killed. I don't know what he did with them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I think put in his full time with the horse logging.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I'm sure he didn't have them when he was killed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then after Adams, what happened, why didn't he keep the place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, I think didn't Camp Adair come in?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Camp Adair come in when Adams was there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] So Adams sold to the government.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But didn't you have another relative in there for a while?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well, that's when. Say, when Les and Grandma Davis lived in there, who owned it then, Adams? No, Adams was the last one in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] My uncle's brother-in-law, Les Davis. Do you want this on tape?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. That's rig/u on school [OSU] properly rig/u there. That's why I'm asking all these questions like where did the mink go. So, Les Davis? Okay. It's going.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, it's going. I didn't know. So, Les Davis was a brother-in-law to Uncle Oswald. So he lived there after Albert was killed, he and his mother lived on the place for some time, I don't remember how long. [Uncle Oswald and Les Davis (brother-in-law) and mother-in-law Davis came from Kansas in 1934. First, they worked at the Wacoma Dairy. Les quit first and moved to Albert Zundt's place and went to work for Valley Mills by the Soap Creek Schoolhouse. About six months later Oswald bought Clarence Wiles' place (about 1936). Les and his mother-in-law moved in with Oswald until Camp Adair came in. Mostly they milked Brown Swiss. The windmill was out of use in later years. Originally, it was for water, but it was replaced in 1932 with an electrical system (home built after World War I) to pump water. The house was powered by about 16 glass batteries stored in the basement. JR]

entries.text: [WILMA] I don't remember how long.

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 24. Harvesting Harding Grass

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Have we got anything on harding grass?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, we never recorded anything on harding grass. We just kept saying we were gonna hit all the harding grass at one time. ***

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Now we're going to talk about harding grass. Mr. Stambaugh raised harding grass for many years. And he, I believe he started in about 1918 to 1920 raising the grass, and he told me that it was brought from Africa by a man by the name of Harding. So it was called harding grass. And he got some seed from him and raised harding grass. And my father used to harvest the harding grass for him, and he'd have to harvest it at night. It bad a head shaped like a wheat head, but with very fine husks and very small seeds. Smaller than a flax seed and oily like a flax seed. And when the grass was ripe those husks would open up a little bit and if you would turn the head upside down when it was perfectly dry the seed would fall out of the husks. So at night when the dew comes on the husks close up tight and then you could bind it with the binder and the seed wouldn't fall out. And then you shocked it upright, as near perfect as you could so it wouldn't fall over. So my father started, he had a binder, and he started harvesting it for Mr. Stambaugh. And sometimes we'd wait till maybe 10:00 before we could start, other times it would be after midnight, and just as soon as the sun came up it would be not very long we would have to quit. So in those days they used horses, and tied a lantern onto the tongue and a couple of lanterns on the binders so they could see, and after in 1928 when my father bought a tractor then we used the tractor on the binder, and we had lights on the tractor. We harvested the grass for Mr. Stambaugh all the time we lived at Camp Adair, and then when Camp Adair was built he bought a farm in Brownsville and planted the grass there and then we harvested it for a number of years after that for Mr. Stambaugh. And after my father died my sister Wilma helped. She rode the binder and I drove the tractor.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Thought we used to have a sled thrasher.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, yes, the thrashing then. Then they would hand thrash it after it sat in the shock for a few days and got good and dry. And they had a sled about 8 foot wide and about 12 foot long with tight bottom and about 12 inch side boards. And you'd have two men take the bundles, pick up the bundles upright from the shock, and put them into the sled. And then they would take the bundles and put them across their knees with the head down and pat the bundles so that the heads would shake back and forth and the seed would drop out of its head. Then they would take the bundles and set them back up in the shock, and so they would do the whole field that way.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] We had a tarp that we had to wrap around.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh, yes, there was a tarp between the sled and the bundle to catch the seed that dropped while we was carrying it to the sled. And after it was all harvested that way then we would hire a thrashing machine to come in and run it through the thrashing machine and it would get a little more seed out of the heads.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Not much, really.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Not much, but I remember back in those days you got about a dollar a pound for the seed and a dollar was worth a lot then. And when the dew went off in the morning and we couldn't bind any more Mrs. Stambaugh, she was a wonderful cook, and she would have a great big meal for all the help.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] During the night they'd bring us out something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh yes, during the night they'd bring us out some snacks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: %Wuu kind of meals would she have?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, she'd fry eggs and you know potatoes, and usually a chocolate cake and stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For breakfast?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Oh, yeah for breakfast.

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] But she always did. I used to see her, but she used to board a lot of people I think in California, cooked in a boarding house didn't she or something? And she'd take three eggs in her hand and she would crack them somehow, and I

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: used to stand there just gawking amazed at her. I have trouble cracking one egg at a time. And she could take three in her hand, and have them somehow, both hands then and she'd have three eggs in one hand and crack them in the skillet, and I'd just stand there with my mouth open and gawk. That amazed me. Them old chocolate cakes, she just whipped them up in a bowl. I've seen her do that, just throw everything in and whip them up. Just put them in an old tin pan you know, and they'd just raise up there like that. They was so good! But she really cooked good.

entries.speaker: narrator-2

entries.speaker: narrator-2

entries.text: [WILMA] But she was a real stern looking woman. Used to, when I was real little, she kind of scared me. But then she was really nice. But that come from being a

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: be kept busy. They stopped running the dairy and the hog farm they operated, too. JR]
bracketed_corrections: [...be kept busy. They stopped running the dairy and the hog farm they operated, too. JR]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you use your own horses or Stainbaugh 's horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No, we used our own horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said one of your horses was blind.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Well, not then I don't think.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well, it was blind for years. Well maybe not during. . . yeah, because I didn't help when you did the horses, so you'd know better.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] No, it was blind later.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Dad used the horses after it was blind for years, didn't he? I mean for raking hay, and mowing and stuff.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Oh yeah, for other work at home. But see 1928 we bought the tractor and then, we started using the tractor. Which was a lot more convenient. Although it took two men to bind, whereas before it just took one man to run the binder and the horses. Took one extra man. And one night we was working on the field, and either the draper needed loosening, I don't remember which, or some harding grass wrapped around the roller, and I had to remove it, one of the two things. So I got, this was on the outside small wheel of the binder. And I got down on my knees, was doing my job there. And pretty soon I started getting stung, and there was a yellow jacket nest in the ground, right where I had my foot. And they crawled up my pant leg. Boy, I sure got stung a lot of times that night.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was one of the dangers of the job then. How come, even though people had to work at night, and even though you had to milk your cows in the morning, that was a lot of money in those days. So it seems like people would have wanted to grow harding grass. Is anyone growing harding grass now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] I don't know of a soul.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] The only one I ever heard of tried to raise it was Dave McPherson.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] And he tried windrowing it and combining it. Lost most of his seed.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] There's none around anywhere. I don't know where you'd even find it in the United States. There must be some somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Stambaugh kind of introduced it. He made a real good living off it.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yes he did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then nobody else could do it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, that's right. And he got it down pat to where he could save most of the seed. I remember Mr. Adams saying, he worked some for Stambaugh, too, you know. And he says, "You know that man's crazy for raising that harding grass. All that work and everything." And I don't remember what I said, but I thought to myself, well he's pretty smart, because he's not working so hard himself. He's hired nearly all of his help. He was getting up there in years then, a long time ago. So he made a good living without working too hard. So he wasn't so darn dumb when you could do that.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] He slept in his Model A out in the field, didn't he, while we was binding. He'd sleep and if you wanted anything, he'd wake up. I mean if you stopped very long or something he'd know you was having trouble. He'd bring us coffee or whatever every so often.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he just kind of had the land and oversaw the operation, but actually farmed out most of the work?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I don't think he touched anything hardly.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Hardly anything. Just managed it.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] I remember when we got that old Dodge pickup, I hauled some harding grass somewhere. Did it go to Jenks? Jenks in Albany or somewhere. And boy he give me a quarter an hour, two-bits an hour, that was as much money as, you know men was making working hard. And I got to set in that pickup and drive over to Jenks. Them sacks was light to load, so it wasn't hard. But he didn't do nothing, I did it all. And he rode with me, but I got paid well for it. Then at Christmas he'd always come around and give us a bonus.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Yeah, he did.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] If he got a good, especially if he got good money, or an extra big crop. Boy that bonus was big. I mean, if you got 50 dollars extra then, that was one pile of money.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] That's the same as 500 now!

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Really, it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that 'd be for the whole family, he'd give your family 50 dollars?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] He'd give each of us!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Each of you 50 dollars?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, I had 50 dollars alone one year, I know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was pretty darn generous.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] He was. If he made money he give it to you. I mean he kept some sure for himself. But he shared it with his help, he did. He was a good old boy, and she was too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On my list here, ahead of time, you've reached today and I didn't have to prompt you. But I want you to tell the story about putting a mouse in his pocket. This guy's so nice, why did you do that?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] That was a few years after Camp Adair. We was over at Brownsville, and old Eddy Richards an old logger was helping us. He lives right over here. And he was, he's kind of a crazy old guy. And old Joe always had twine and stuff in his pocket for his cramps on his legs and stuff. So Eddie Richards one day, somebody killed a mouse, and picked it up and pulled his back pocket open and flipped it in there. Well after a couple of days; Joe wore his same overalls for a few days. Old Ed, he says, "We're gonna have to tell him, it's gonna start smelling pretty soon." We let it go for a little while longer and pretty quick, I don't know why, he wanted some string out of his back pocket to tie harding grass sack or something shut with. He reached in there and grabbed that old string and he grabbed the mouse instead and he flipped it out and let out a yell and nobody told; he kept wondering how that dang mouse got in there, but he never did know. That was funny, I always think of old Eddie Richards, he was ornery. [Being an old logger he was quite a prankster. WR]
bracketed_corrections: [Being an old logger he was quite a prankster. WR]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was Mr. Stambaugh the type of guy that you played practical jokes on or was he the type of person that didn't like them too well?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well, it didn't bother him I don't think. He still don't know or never did know I don't think how that dead mouse got in there. But we just stood around there and laughed our fool heads off. Of course we knew, I seen old Eddie grab the back of his pocket, just pull it out and drop that mouse daintily in. And it was still in, I thought maybe it would gone out, or he'd found it you know while we were Out

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: harvesting or something, cause it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] He was one of the first, I believe that planted grass in rows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh people didn't.. . you were telling me that before, that where you planted in rows you made good money, and where you broadcast you didn't. But he was one of the first people to plant any type of grass in rows? Was that unusual?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] It was unusual then.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Real unusual. That's the first grass I ever seen in rows.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] But they do plant orchard grass quite a lot in rows now. They didn't used to.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] They plant quite a few different things in rows now. There's two or three different grasses.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Seems to yield better, you know, it has some bare space.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Fescue does too, the tall fescue does better in rows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was kind of an innovator not only bringing in a new crop, but planting in rows?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, that was the first I ever seen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he started planting in rows maybe sometime a little after World War I? With grass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] When he first started. He started in rows. And it wasn't until about the '40's that or later than the '40's before we ever saw any other grass field in rows.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Well I never seen any in rows until, really until Bethel Vernon down here. We planted orchard grass.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [JAKE] Was that in the '40's? Late '40's?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Yeah, it was after we moved. That was the first. Then Bud and I harvested that orchard grass in rows. That was the first I'd seen in rows. Besides Stambaugh's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How come your family didn't plant harding grass in rows, f he was doing so well?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [WILMA] Because we was dairy, used all our land pretty much for dairy. And then up on the hill I don't think it grew good, it dried out. We raised hairy vetch up there. [In 1930-33 we grew navy beans, 14-15 acres. Hand-pulled at 3 cents/lb. Then we bought an old bean thrasher -- a 24-inch wide bean thrasher, head high. In the seed catalog was "White Mexican" or "Prolific Three Bean" --5 lbs. of seed makes 315 lbs of beans. I still have some of the seed. JR]
